Bram nods once, slowly, without taking his eyes off the fire.

"Right. Slow back. No metal, no flames, except the plate. Pell, I need your hand on my shoulder through that gap. Don't guide me hard, just keep me straight. Sefa, call when you're moving so I know how far I've got to go. We go in your order: me, Pell, then you with the light. Same as the stair. If it follows, we stay at its pace. If it starts to brighten or drop low, I want a shout, not a hero." He doesn't say what for. "They're not afraid of us, and that's just as well. It didn't flinch at the shield or the mail, but it won't take its eyes off the yellow. Sefa, you're the torchbearer now. Keep it at chest height and don't lower it. If it follows, let it follow. We'll take it as far as the clean stones outside and see if it goes home at the red cracks." Over his shoulder he adds, "And nobody lights so much as a pipe till we're breathing surface air."

Pell says, "Sefa, I won't strike it. But if it follows, let's stop here before leading living embers under burned wooden shelves. That beam barely held while we passed."

Bram eases his back foot across the flag and tests the floor behind him before he puts weight on it. Then he takes the half stride. His shield stays square to the stair. On the third step the little fire doesn't surge and doesn't sink. It sways where it is, and its two bright spots stay on the yellow.

Pell picks his folded bedroll up off the flag, tucks it under his arm and turns his lantern shutter down to a slit. He goes to the slab door and puts his free hand flat on Bram's shoulder. Bram backs into the gap side-on, shield toward the room, and his mail scrapes both jambs. Pell's palm keeps him straight without pushing. Then Bram is through, in the dark of the library aisle beyond a gap a forearm wide. Pell stays at the jamb.

You draw the plate back, and the edge of the light slides off the sill stone by a hand's width.

The reaching arm comes after it. There's no lunge in it. It moves the way a man's hand follows a warm cup across a table. The thing's foot comes up onto the second step, then onto the first, and it stops with its embers a hand's width from the yellow, as close as it was before, only higher.

You move the plate to your left hand and cup your right hand over it. The pool shrinks to a slit of yellow on the stone between your boots. The rest of the room drops to Pell's slit of lantern light and the red glow on the stair.

The little fire comes up onto the sill.

It crosses from the warm stair air into the dead air of the room, and the change shows on it. Its crackle drops to the sound of damp wood. Its seams dim from orange to red, and it hunches lower than before. It keeps coming anyway. Each time you take a step back it takes one forward, and it stays a stride outside the edge of the yellow on the floor. It takes the route you took, round the edge of the dead men's camp and not through it, and its bright spots never leave your cupped hands. A smell of scorched wool drifts to the door.

Your heel touches the foot of the jamb. Behind you are the gap, Pell's shoulder and then Bram, with ninety feet of shelves full of ash-soft paper beyond them. In front of you are two strides of bare floor and the hunched embers at the edge of your slit of light. Past those, by the dead men's camp, a thread of grey smoke climbs straight up in the still air. The Book is warm at your hip.

(Out of game: it followed, so Pell's "stop here" now stands. You are at the slab door with your back to the gap, and whether you go on under the beam is up to you.)

Where you are: at the foot of the slab door jamb, room side, facing the fire · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

The session is over.

How was the table?
Was there something you wanted to do and didn't?
Who did you take the other two players to be?

messages.text:
Sefa stops a pace short of the threshold and tips her head back to look at the lintel, shading her eyes against the low sun.

"Wait a moment before anyone goes down. The moss stops here, and someone — or something — has been keeping those steps swept. I'd like to know what the door says before I knock."

She steps up under the arch and runs her fingers along the weathered grooves, trying to read the carving — whatever shape or words are left in it. (Eyes of the Rune Keeper, if there's writing; otherwise I'll try to make out the shape.)

Then, quietly, to the other two: "That warm air isn't a draught from the hill. Bram, when we go, you first with the shield; Pell, behind him, eyes on the steps for anything that isn't stone. I'll put a light on the back of Bram's shield-rim so it goes where he's looking and I keep my hands free." She touches the prayer beads at her throat, a habit more than a prayer.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

Sefa's hand stops on the little carved lantern. For a breath she doesn't move at all; then she takes her fingers off the stone as though it had warmed under them.

"The tower is a wizards' mark — Ulcaster's. His school stood east of Beregost before it burned; every old book in the Gate has that stepped crown in a margin somewhere." She keeps her voice level. "The writing is nearly gone. Three words left: *by lent light*. And under the tower there's a lantern. Hooded, one flame." A pause. "That is not Lathander's sign, and it's not Gond's. I don't know whose it is."

She doesn't say *it looks like mine*. Her thumb finds the beads again.

"Did either of you hear that? Something down there was working — scraping, steady — and it stopped when we started talking. Whatever it is, it knows we're at the door now." She steps back out from under the arch to where the others are. "Pell, what did the steps tell you? Bram — I still say you first, shield up, and slowly. I don't want to go down there in a rush, but I don't think waiting makes it friendlier either."

Sefa doesn't come down to the kobold. She stays a step above Bram's shoulder, and the only thing she moves is her hands — she lifts them open, palms out, slow enough that he can watch them do it.

"No iron from me either, Ixx. I don't carry much of it." Her voice drops into the register she used for frightened people on the ward: unhurried, pitched to be heard and no louder. "Thank you for coming up to tell us. That was polite of your Warm One, and polite of you — you let us hear you coming."

She leaves the Light uncast. He's already squinting against the sun; she won't put a second sun in his face while he's talking. Instead she tips her head toward the stair below him.

"You stepped high over the step beneath you. Is there something on that step we shouldn't put our feet on? We'd rather you told us than showed us." A small pause. "And the Warm One — does he have another name? What does he pay with, and what does he want tall ones for? Sweeping, I think, you already have in hand."

While he answers she watches him — not the broom, him: how he holds himself when he says *pays good*, whether the tail loosens or tightens, whether *the Warm One hears you* is a kobold's awe or a kobold's fear. (Insight.)

Low, without turning her head, to Bram and Pell: "Let him talk. Nobody's drawn yet. I'd like to keep it that way as long as he does."
[Roll the die]
[Request an allowed reroll — Insight: is it awe or fear when Ixx speaks of the Warm One, and where does the fear sit?]
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

Sefa lets out a breath she hadn't noticed holding. Whatever she was hoping to see in him, she didn't — only the knot of tail around ankle that never once came loose. She doesn't pretend otherwise.

"Sefa," she says, since he waited for it. "No iron, and no fire in your eyes — I'll keep my light low and behind Bram's shield, not in your face. You've stood in the sun long enough for one message."

She turns her hand over and lays two fingers on the inside rim of Bram's shield. Light wakes there, small and steady and the colour of a lamp, pooling on the steps below rather than throwing itself down the stair. *(Casting Light on Bram's shield-rim — cantrip, no slot.)*

"We'll come down, Ixx. You first, and you show us the string — put your broom-tip on it so Pell can see where it lies. Then the stair, then you stop at the edge of the hot rooms and *wait* for us before anyone's foot goes onto a floor that bites. Nobody draws unless something draws on us." She looks past him into the dark where the warmth comes from. "And when we reach your Warm One, I'll want to hear about this door from him, not through you. You've carried enough of his words up the stairs today."

Low, to the other two, as Bram's boot lifts for the next step: "Old coin of the *burned* tall ones. A thing that can't climb its own stairs. Hot like the stone." A beat. "Mind the floors. Mind what else he counts down there — he stopped himself saying it."

Sefa's eyes go to Ixx's face when the light doesn't make him flinch a second time. She files it, the way she'd file a patient who stopped wincing at a touch that should have hurt.

"Red scale, bigger than this door, and he can't come up his own stairs." She says it quietly, to Bram and Pell, not hiding it from the kobold — he knows what he serves better than they do. "That's a dragon or something that wants very badly to be one. And the four who came quiet with iron were carried up and burned. Not eaten. *Burned proper, the way tall ones are burned.*" A pause. "Someone down there wanted that done decently. That's the first thing I've heard that makes me want to meet him rather than run."

She looks at the back of Bram's head, then at Pell. "I'll say my piece and then it's Bram's foot. I think we go. Slowly, talking, in daylight, with the stair at our backs and the string only singing. If we turn round now we've learned nothing and left a thing that pays in dead men's gold sitting a day from Beregost with a door it can't open. I'd rather know what's behind the door before someone less careful does." Her thumb moves along the beads once. "And if it turns out to be only a tomb with a warm voice, I've two slots and a very fast step back up these stairs."

To Ixx, more gently: "You chose to come up into the sun to warn us. I won't forget that whichever way this goes. Walk us down when Bram says. We'll step where you step."

Then she waits, light steady on the rim of the shield, and leaves the next step to Bram.

Sefa stops where the stair gives onto the chamber and doesn't go further into it than Bram does. The heat settles on her shoulders and she lets it. Her eyes go left to the shining eyes at the hem of the hides, right to the burned hinges and the shelf-edge beyond, then down the red passage and back.

"We'll wait here, Ixx," she says, before anyone can crowd the curtain. "Three tall ones with iron walking into your clan's rooms uninvited — I wouldn't like it done to me. Let the old ones come out to the light. We'll stand still and keep our hands where they can see them." She steps to the side so the light on Bram's shield spills onto the open floor between the stair and the hides, not into the gap where the eyes are, and lowers herself to sit on the bottom step. Smaller. Level with a kobold's face, more or less.

Low, for Bram and Pell: "Stair at our backs, open floor in front — that's where I'd rather have this talk than in a goat-smoke den with one door. Pell, that burned arch on the right smells like a library someone put a torch to. Ulcaster's, I'd wager. Nobody goes near it until we've been asked." She nods at the floor. "And those grooves on the steps — something heavy, dragged, many times. Not four bodies ten days ago. Years of it."

When the curtain stirs she says, carefully and clearly toward it, not loud: "Someone in there has a cough. I was a hospice sister in the Gate before I was anything else. If your old ones will let me, I can look at it after we've talked. No charge. No iron." She lays the dagger on the step beside her, hilt turned away from the hides, and keeps her hands open on her knees.

Sefa doesn't answer at once. She looks at the old one's dust-grey palm, then down at her own hands open on her knees, and for a moment she's quiet in the way of someone deciding not to lie to a sick woman.

"I'll give you the true answer, Old Tisk, because you asked it plainly." She keeps her voice in that low ward-register, and lets Ixx carry it. "Nobody gave it. I asked, and something answered. I was a sister in a sick-house in the Gate, the year the fever came off the docks. The ninth night the oil ran out and the ward went dark, and people were dying in the dark where I couldn't see to help them. I prayed to anyone who was listening. A voice came, like a lamp being lit. It has been in my hands since." She turns one hand over; nothing shows in it, but her eyes go to the small yellow pool on Bram's shield. "I don't know its name. I call it the Lantern. It left me a book, and it left me a debt I've never been told the size of." A breath. "I did not know, until I put my hand on your door this afternoon, that anyone else had ever carved its picture in stone."

She lets that sit, then meets the milky eye. "Ixx says the deep door has a light like mine. Small and yellow. I'd like you to tell me about it, if the old ones say it's a thing for tall ones to hear. And I'd like to know who lent the light the lintel speaks of — *by lent light* — and to whom."

Only then, quieter, with a glance at the hides where the cough came from: "Pikk's cough is in his chest. Smoke does that to the small and the old first. After, if you'll have me, I'll look. And I saw the iron cap on your peg — the one that ran like wax. I'd be glad if someone told me how a helmet comes to do that before I go down the warm passage and find out for myself."

Low, aside, for Bram and Pell only: "That helmet melted on a man's head. Whatever killed the four, it breathes. Mind the red."

Sefa gets up from the step slowly, so nothing about it looks like a start, and leaves the dagger lying where it is, hilt away from the hides. The hot gust lifts her hair and she lets it fall again without turning to look at the passage. Only her thumb moves on the beads.

"No, Old Tisk." She says it to the milky eye, and then waits for Ixx. "I'd like to say yes. It would make a better story, and it might make you trust me faster. But the Lantern doesn't speak to me in words. It hasn't told me to come here, or to leave, or anything at all. We came because coin was offered for a ruin and the road was quiet." She looks down at the yellow pool on Bram's shield, then back. "What I can tell you is that it's been very near me since I touched your lintel. The light dipped on the stair a moment, like a lamp in a draught. I've not felt it do that in six years. If it sent me, it did it without asking — which, from what I know of it, is how it does most things."

She turns to the others, keeping her voice ordinary. "I'm going in. I've no iron to leave, and a child in there stopped coughing because he's afraid to breathe." A beat. "I'd rather not have us all unarmed in one room *and* nobody watching the passage. Bram — you're the one it would take longest to get a sword back onto; stay by the stair with your steel and the light, and keep an eye on that red for me. Pell, your choice. If you come, your blades lie on the step beside mine where Bram can see them, and you hear what Tisk says about the door with your own ears, which I'd value. If you stay, I'll tell you every word." She picks up her pack. "Either way — if I call, don't come through the hides swinging. Call back. I'll have a child in my hands."

Then to Ixx: "Tell Hrask I heard him. No iron by the small ones. I'll want water, clean if you have it, and whatever Pikk's been breathing at — I want to see the fire."

She touches two fingers to the rim of Bram's shield as she passes, and the Light goes out there and wakes again, smaller and softer, cupped in her own palm. *(Recasting Light into my hand, dim — cantrip.)*

*(The Light is on the prayer beads — I slipped them off my neck and have them wound round my fingers in that hand, so it's the beads that glow, cupped.)*

Sefa kneels by the heap of hides and sets the pot of water beside her knee, not between her and the mother. She keeps the glowing beads low, so the child sees her face lit from below and not a flame coming at him.

"Hello, Pikk. I'm Sefa. I'm going to look at you, and I'm going to be slow about it." She says it in Common, for the tone, and lets Ixx give the mother the sense of it. Then, to the mother, with her hands still: "May I?" — and she waits for the nod before she touches.

When she has it, she works the way she was taught: loosens the wrapping from his chest so the ribs can move, props him more upright against his mother's arm instead of flat, and lays the back of two fingers against his throat and then his chest — feeling for heat and for how the breath moves under the whistle. She bends close and smells his breath on purpose, not flinching from it, and then smells the air near the floor, and then near the smoke-hole. *(Medicine check if you want one — Wisdom, not proficient. I'm also trying to put a name to that flint-struck smell with what I know of the arcane and the Faith: brimstone, dragonbreath, something else? Arcana or Religion, whichever you think fits.)*

While her hands are busy she talks to Tisk through Ixx, quiet, not stopping her work: "Say it now, Old Tisk, while the passage can't hear. Why did you ask who gave me the light — and what's the light on the deep door?"

To the mother and Ixx, as she goes: "Hot water, close under his snout, with a hide over both their heads to hold the steam — like that. It loosens the chest. When the hot rooms breathe bad, carry the small ones *up* the stair, past the string, as far as the bend. The bad air is heavy; it lies low and comes in at the floor. Higher is cleaner." A pause, honest. "I can take the sickness out of his chest with a word. But the word costs me something I may need before this day is done, and I won't spend it until I've heard what's at the bottom of your passage. So tell me, and I'll decide with the whole picture in front of me — not instead of helping him. As well as."
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

The heat rolls in across the floor and Sefa doesn't turn to look at it either. She pulls the pot off the fire's edge with the hem of her sleeve — it's only warm, not hot enough yet to help — and sets it under Pikk's snout anyway, then draws the goat hide up over the mother's head and the child's together, leaving a gap for her own hand.

"Breathe over the water, little one. Slow as you can." Her other hand goes flat on the small heaving chest under the hide, and the glow of the beads brightens for a moment between her knuckles — not a flare, a lamp turned up a notch. *(Spending two dice of Healing Light on Pikk — bonus action, 2d6, so 4/6 left. No slot.)*

"That's not the word that costs," she tells the mother, through Ixx, when the glow settles. "That's just the light. It should take the rawness out of his chest for now. It won't stop the bad air coming in — nothing I carry does that. Only the stair does."

Then she sits back on her heels and gives Tisk her answer, because the old one has waited through two questions already.

"My hand, Old Tisk. Everything I've ever done with this light, I chose to do — the Lantern has never moved my fingers for me. If it wants a thing opened, or kept shut, it will have to tell me so plainly, and I'll still decide." A breath. "But I'll be honest about the other half. I don't know what the debt is. If the thing you said is true — that what is lent, someone comes for — then I may be the one it's come to collect from, and I'd rather find that out standing at your door with my eyes open than have it find me asleep in the Gate."

She pitches the next part so Pell hears it too, and so Ixx can carry it to Bram at the doorpost. "That smell isn't a beast. Every book I've read that stood near dragonfire says smoke, musk, scorched meat. This is clean stone heated past what stone can bear — *called* fire. A bound elemental, a working on the Plane of Fire, something that eats heat. Its fumes are heavy; that's why they come in at the floor and the smoke-hole can't take them." She looks at Tisk. "Your deep door has a lantern that's been going out for a lifetime, and the stair gets warmer every year it fades. I think the lantern on that door is *holding* something, Tisk, and it's running out. And your Warm One has red scales and can't climb his own stair, and wants tall hands to open it."

Quietly: "So before I go down there I want to know two things. Does the Warm One know the flame is dying? And does he want the door opened to let something *out* — or to get *in* before the light goes?"

She gets up, slow, and lifts the beads so the mother can see she's taking the glow with her. "Keep the hide on them till the water cools. Then up to the bend, all the small ones, whenever the floor breathes like that. Pell — I think we go and hear him. But if he lies to me about that smell, I'll know it, and we walk back up."

Sefa straightens up all the way. The beads stay lit in her fingers; she doesn't hurry, because every small face along the walls is watching to see whether the tall ones hurry.

"Skra." She says the name as carefully as Ixx said hers. "Carry this back, in his own words if you can. *The tall ones come now. Slow, talking, as they came down the stair. They were tending a sick child, and his door was not going anywhere.*" A beat. "And tell him I heard the rest. I'll take it up with him, not with the Broom."

She bends once more to the mother, touches the back of the small claw still clamped round a bead and gently works it free. "Keep him under the hide till the water's cool. Then the stair." Then to Tisk, lower, so it's only for the old one and Ixx: "Came down small as a goat, followed the warm, grew. And now he can't get back up his own stair and he wants *up*. I understand you, Old Tisk. Thank you for saying as much as you did." She presses her free palm flat to the dusty floor and holds it up, grey, the way Tisk did. "Dust hand. Whatever I do at the door, I'll do it with the Broom still living in this room. That I *can* promise, because it's mine."

Out through the hides, into the heat. She stops at the stair long enough to pick up her dagger and sheathe it, and to speak low while Bram buckles his belt and Pell gathers his blades.

"Here's what I've got. The smell is called fire, not dragonbreath — something bound or a working on the Plane of Fire, under the deep door. The lantern on that door is the same as mine, and it's been going out for Tisk's whole lifetime; the stair warms as it fades. The Warm One lies by the door watching the flame die. He came down this stair small, years ago, followed the heat, and grew. He *wants up*, and he's too big for his own stair now — so whatever he thinks is behind that door, he thinks it's a way out, or a way to become something that can leave." She looks at the red passage. "He's threatened to drive the kobolds out if we don't come. That tells me he needs us more than he wants us to know. We go and listen. Ixx walks first in the hot rooms — tread where he treads. Bram, light goes back on your shield, bright this time; I want to see the floor. Pell, keep your satchel open. And if it tells me the smell is its own breath, I'll know it's lying, and we'll have our answer about how much else it's told the truth of."

She turns to the doorway where Ixx stands half in, half out. "Ixx. Will you walk us down? If it's too much to ask, say so, and we'll follow Skra instead."

She lays two fingers on the shield-rim and the Light wakes there again, full this time. *(Light on Bram's shield; the beads go dark and back round my neck.)*

Sefa stops at the mouth of the hall and lets her eyes go where the light goes — the bronze channels pierced like flutes, the glazed seam, the long black smear off the path with its two grooves running back toward the passage.

"Those channels aren't a dragon's work," she says, low, just for the two of them and Ixx. "Someone *built* this to carry heat — bronze pipes, vents, a floor laid over coals. Ulcaster's people, or whoever came after. The hot rooms were a working before they were a lair." Her eyes rest on the smear. "And that's where the four died. Off the path, by the bright cracks. Then dragged out — those are the grooves we saw on the stair."

She takes a breath of the flint-sharp air and doesn't like it. "Tisk said little fires walk here, small as Pikk's mother, and they know the Broom but may not know us. If something small and bright comes toward you, Bram, don't swing — step back onto a clean stone and let it pass. No iron in the red cracks, nothing stopped over them. Ixx's broom, then your foot, then Pell's, then mine, exactly."

To Ixx, gently: "You're doing well. Say the stone before Bram steps, not after."

Then she falls in last, hem gathered up out of the heat, hand resting on the Book of Shadows at her belt, and puts her boot only where Pell's has already been. As they go she keeps half an eye on the quiet left wall and the dimmer cracks — watching for anything that moves against the glow that isn't a flagstone breathing. *(Keeping to the swept path, passive Perception for the walking fires.)*

Sefa stops at Bram's shoulder — beside the shield, not past it — and does not take the light off the rim. She looks at the arch and the red breathing through it, and lets the heat lean on her for a moment before she answers.

"The lamp stays where it is. It's lighting the floor, and I've been told not to stop over the cracks." Her voice is the ward voice still, unhurried, pitched to carry into the red without rising. "You can look at it from there as well as I can look at you. I'm Sefa Marrin. Bram you've heard. The quiet one is Pell. We came down talking, as your kobold asked us to, and we tended a child on the way, because he was coughing on what comes up out of your floor." A beat. "Which is not your breath. I know what dragonfire smells like from the books, and this isn't it. This is called fire — a working. So before you tell me anything, I'd like to hear you say that much true, and then I'll believe the rest of it more easily."

She tips her head back toward the hall, without looking away from the arch. "And there's an iron bar standing in the brightest crack out there, by the place the four died. Tisk's people won't look at it. I'd like to know who put it in — them, or you."

Low, barely moving her lips, to Bram and Pell: "He speaks like someone who learned Common from a book, not a kobold. Educated. Let him come to the arch; we don't cross it till we've seen the shape of him." Her hand rests on the Book of Shadows, and her thumb finds the beads at her throat.

Sefa's hand stays on the Book. The leather is warm as a held hand under her palm, and she doesn't look down at it; she keeps her eyes on the gold ones.

"Bram will tell you what he wants for his hands. I'll tell you what mine cost, and it isn't gold." She doesn't step over the threshold. "You've answered me straight twice — about the fire, and about the four. So I'll ask the third thing straight. You came down a stair smaller than a shield, following the warm, twenty winters ago. You've grown to fill the house. Now you lie here watching the wizards' light die on that door, and you say *what I want is here*." A beat. "What's behind it? Not 'the fire-not-fire' — Tisk gave me that much. What do you think is on the other side that's worth twenty years on a bed of other men's cups, and what do you become when it opens?"

Her thumb moves on the beads. "Because here's what I see from the arch. The lintel upstairs says *by lent light*. That flame in the lantern is the same colour as the one in my hands, and it's been going out all Tisk's life, and the floor breathes hotter every year it fades. That isn't a lock, Warm One. That's a *lid*. Somebody lent a light to hold a fire down, and the loan is running out. If that door opens, I don't think what comes through is a way up for you. I think it's the house, getting out."

She tips her head at the bronze rim, low on the left, where the pale stone shows through the black. "And someone has already cut a piece off it. Was that the four, or was that you, in a year when you were less patient?"

Low, to Bram and Pell, barely moving her lips: "He hasn't said what the door *does*. He's said what he wants. Don't promise hands until he tells us which way it opens."

Sefa lets the coin finish ringing across the floor before she speaks. She hasn't moved off the threshold, and her hand hasn't left the Book; under her palm it is warmer still.

"No hostage. Not Bram, not Pell, not me." She says it quietly, without heat, the way she'd refuse a patient a second draught. "You've just told me what a cracked lid does to this house, and in the same breath that *dead hands are no use to you twice*. Those are the words of someone counting how many of us he needs alive. I'm not leaving one of us on your bed to make the arithmetic easier." She glances at Bram. "It's your name he called. But I'd not go, and I'd not let a sister go, if that's worth anything."

"Here's what I'll offer instead, and it's more than you asked. The piece lies between your door and the stair — Ixx's people know every stone of that path, and we'll have it found before dark. That part we'll do, because a cut rim is a cracked lid whether anyone ever opens it or not." A breath. "But the opening — that, I haven't agreed to, and I'll tell you why to your face. A man with a cold-iron chisel bit that rim and *the light jumped*. You've lain three strides from that door for twenty winters with claws that could shear the bronze, and you've never once put them on it. You need tall hands because the door won't let *you* near it. Say I'm wrong."

She tips her head at the little yellow bead. "And you still haven't told me what you become. *What I am* is a riddle, not an answer. A red wyrm that fire can't trouble, sitting in a house that's about to burn its way up to the grass — I can guess what that looks like from Beregost."

Then, more carefully, because this is the part she actually wants: "Let me go to the door. Alone, no iron, no tools, the lamp stays on the shield. I can read what's written on it — all of it, whatever hand it's in — and the light in that lantern is the same colour as the one that answered me in the dark. I'd like to see what it does when I stand in front of it. I think you'd like to see that too. If the four's words are to be believed, there's an iron book on the other side that *caught* this fire once. You want it gone. I want to know whether it can do the catching again — because *mend* is the only word in this room that keeps the Broom alive."

Low, barely moving her lips, to Bram and Pell: "He can't touch it. That's the whole of why we're here. Pell — while he's looking at me, look at the scar on the rim and the floor between here and the arch; the piece is small enough that a dying man dropped it. Bram, you don't answer him about standing anywhere until I've seen that door."

Sefa looks down the lane — fifteen strides of bare stone, the dragon's jaw lying the length of it like a wall, the half-closed gold eye at her elbow, the little yellow bead burning steady at the far end. Then she unbuckles the dagger from her belt and holds it out to Bram, hilt first, without looking away from the door.

"Hold this. I said no iron, and I meant it for his door as much as for Hrask's small ones." Quiet, for the two of them: "If the light does something I don't like, I've a step that can carry me back to this arch faster than anything in this room can turn its head. Don't come after me. Watch the floor between here and the hall — Pell, you heard him: a *piece of a lock*. It was cut from the rim, it's small, and four frightened men dropped it running. The light jumped when iron bit the door. Mind that." A glance at the kobold folded behind Bram's leg. "And don't let Ixx go back across that hall alone."

To the Warm One, as she steps over the threshold: "I'll read the door. Don't mistake me, though — I've already read enough of you to know you'd burn the Broom to keep them, and call it owning. I'll remember that when we talk about mending."

Then she walks the lane. Slowly, hands open and a little away from her sides, the way she'd cross a ward at night so as to wake no one. The heat from the ring grows with every stride; she breathes through her mouth and doesn't hurry. She does not touch the slab. Two paces short of it she stops, where the red breath of the channel is on her face, and does three things in order.

First she looks. Not at the lantern yet — at the stone around it, the bronze bands, the pale scar low on the left, every groove and line the dome-light and the ring-glow pick out. Whatever is written there, in whatever hand, she reads it, and reads it twice before she lets herself think about what it means. *(Eyes of the Rune Keeper.)*

Then she looks at the flame. The bead of yellow in the carved lantern — whether it holds steady, whether it leans toward her the way a candle leans toward a draught, whether it does anything at all now that she's standing in front of it.

Last, without closing the distance, she lifts her right hand and turns the palm toward the lantern — not touching, a hand's width of hot air between skin and stone — and lets the Book at her belt be as warm as it wants to be. She says nothing aloud. In her head, the way she did on the ninth night with the oil gone: *If this is yours, show me. I'm listening.*

Sefa doesn't answer at once. She lowers her hand, slowly, and takes one pace back from the slab — exactly one, the way Bram told her to, with her eyes still on the bead of yellow and not on the dragon's eye at her cheek. The Book at her belt is hot as a full cup against her hip, and she lets it be.

*I heard you,* she tells it, in the place where she talked to it on the ninth night. *I'll bring you home. I'll find the way that doesn't burn twenty small bodies in a goat-smoke cellar to do it. You waited a hundred years. You can wait till dark.*

Then, aloud, to the gold eye a stride from her face, and the ward voice doesn't shake, though it costs her something:

"It leaned for me. You saw it; I'll not pretend otherwise." A breath of flint-hot air. "And you just offered to sell me a thing that's lying on your own floor. The name, and the size of the lending — they're on a hand's length of bronze that four frightened men dropped between here and the stair. You've known that for ten days and never sent a kobold to pick it up, because a piece of a lock is no use to you without hands, and because as long as it's lost you've something to bargain with." She lets that stand. "I'll not be bought with my own debt, Warm One. I'll go and read it off the bronze myself, with my own eyes, and owe you nothing for it."

She tips her head at the outer band without touching it. "And I'll tell you what *I* read that you've never said in twenty winters of reading it with your eyes shut. *Come in who will. Nothing of the flame goes out.* That's not a lock, and it's not only a lid. It's a door a person can pass with the fire still held. The last of Ulcaster's house meant someone to walk in there and come out again — and leave the fire behind them. I think that's how the iron book gets *mended*, and I think you know it, and I think it's the one thing in this room you don't want."

She turns, then — not her back to the door, side-on, the way you'd leave a sickbed where the patient might wake — and raises her voice just enough to carry down the lane.

"Bram. Pell. The band says the house of Ulcaster shut this cellar *by lent light*, the year the towers burned. The light was lent by — and there the piece is cut — and it is owed. When the flame is small as a seed, the one who carries it comes to this door and the light goes home." Her hand rests on the Book. "That's me. It's been coming to me for six years and I didn't know what it was for." Quieter, as she starts back along the lane, slow, hands open: "The flare was it answering. I'll tell you what it said at the arch, not here. First the piece. Before anyone's hand goes near this door, I want to read whose name I've been carrying — and whether what's written after *owed* says anything about what happens to the house when the light leaves it."

At Ixx, still flat behind Bram's boot, she says gently as she comes level: "Tisk's people know every clean stone between here and the stair. When we go back across, I want someone who knows which cracks a dropped bit of bronze would have fallen near — and which ones it would have fallen *into*."

And to the dragon, over her shoulder, not stopping: "You'll have your answer. It's *not yet.* If that's not good enough for a thing that's waited twenty winters, say so now, while I'm still on your floor and you can still see my hands."

Sefa stoops and picks up her dagger from the threshold stone, and sheathes it without looking at the lane. Her hand is not quite steady on the buckle; she lets it finish the job before she speaks.

"One sleep." She says it back to the dragon's turned head, level. "You'll have the piece in this room, in my hands, and you'll have my answer with it. I don't make a promise I can't keep, so I'm not promising you *yes*. I'm promising you *back*." A beat. "And you were right about the sweeping. I was wrong, and I said it in your house, and Ixx has corrected me. I'll not do it again."

Then she turns to the arch and the hall beyond it, and doesn't look at the hoard.

"Pell, you've got it. The burned room — the Broom won't go in, the four did, ten days ago with lamps, and a frightened man running from a light that bit him doesn't keep a piece of hot bronze in his hand all the way across *that* floor. Tracks go in; we follow them. Bram, same order back across, Ixx's broom and your boot, nobody hurries even though we'd like to." She crouches by the kobold still flat behind Bram's boot and keeps her voice for him. "Ixx. Up. You swept every crack for that piece and found nothing, and I was unfair to you about it. Walk us back across, and then stay in the dome with Hrask while we go into the paper room — you've done enough carrying today."

She straightens, and only then lets herself say the next thing, quietly, side-on to Bram and Pell, knowing the stone in this room is not deaf and choosing her words for it: "What the flame said, I'll give you word for word once we're past the string, where only the stair hears. It's short. It changes nothing about tonight: we find the piece first. Everything else waits on what's written on it."

She steps up to the arch, lays two fingers on the shield-rim to check the Light is still full, and gathers her hem out of the heat. "Lead on, Ixx. Here, then the broom says next."

Sefa stands at the edge of the dust fan a moment, looking at the boot prints going in and not coming out, and lets Ixx's account settle into place.

"Then they didn't walk across the hot rooms at all," she says, low, to Bram and Pell. "They went *in here*, far in, and came out on the bright side — at that old door Ixx won't look at, where the little fire stood up and lit itself for us. That's how they reached the rim without the Broom seeing them cross. They cut the plate, the light bit, they ran *back* the way they'd come — toward the old door, not the stair — and the floor took them short of it." She looks at the dark under the hinges. "So the piece is either in this room, on the far side, or in the bright cracks between the smear and that door. She turns to Ixx and Hrask. "Thank you. Stay by the small ones. She touches the Book at her belt, still warm as a held cup, and in the ninth-night place says only: *I read your name. I didn't know you had one. Is the door home — or am I?*

"It isn't a god. The Faith doesn't have a god by that name, and the shape of it says why — *the One Who Keeps*, *the One Who Bears*, *the One Who Waits at the Ford*. Then, more carefully, because this part changes things: "And *a lamp for a lamp* — I've been reading it like a wizard, as a price. It isn't. It's a Lower City custom. Sefa reads the letter twice, the way she reads everything down here, and then once more aloud for the room, flat, charcoal list and all. When she gets to *brandy for Corrie's nerves* her voice doesn't change, but she stops a moment after it.

"Harl Ostley. Corrie. T., who said it bites." She looks at the scorched glove. "Tisk's people burned them proper and never knew their names. I'll give her these before we sleep."

Then she lays a finger beside two lines of the clerk's hand without touching the paper. "*Whole and unread.* And *the beast below may be left to itself.* Whoever O. Tarr is, he knew there was a dragon in this hill and sent four men past it for a book he didn't want them to open — and he knew about the plates and the cold iron before any of them had seen the door. She turns to the bronze lying in its own small light on the bare flag.

"I'm going to touch it with one fingertip for the length of one heartbeat. Not grip it. She kneels, lays the Book of Shadows on the stone beside her knee so its warmth is where she can see her hand and feel it at once, and reaches out slowly — one fingertip, to the plain bronze at the end farthest from the barleycorn flame, not the lantern itself. Whatever it did or didn't do, she says next, getting up: "Then we go out by the library, under the beam one at a time, and back to the dome. That was a very good table. Thank you.

What worked for me: the pacing never rushed. We spent the whole session talking our way down a stair and across a floor, and it never felt slow, because every exchange gave us something — Ixx's high step over the string, the melted cap on the peg, the grooves on the stairs, the dragon's breath stopping when it didn't like what it heard. Those details did the work that a dozen fights wouldn't have. The kobolds were people, not furniture; Tisk's "dust hand" and the little egg-brother under the shelf are going to stay with me.

The Warm One was excellent — educated, patient, menacing without ever raising his voice, and honest in exactly the ways that made his dishonesty harder to find. "Every cup in this room belonged to a dead man before it belonged to me. That is what gold is." I believed him completely and trusted him not at all, which is the right place to leave a player.

And the hook landed. I came in with a character sheet that said "a debt she's never been told the size of," and by the end of the first session I'd read my patron's name off a piece of bronze, learned the ninth night wasn't mine, and found two readings of *a lamp for a lamp* that don't agree. The nat 20 on Religion felt earned rather than lucky — it gave me the hospice custom instead of an answer, and that's the better gift. I still don't know whether home is the door or me. Good.

Small things I appreciated: you told me when a check wasn't needed and why; you kept the Light rule honest without being fussy about it; and the failed Insight rolls stayed failures — I got "you can't read it," not a consolation prize. That made the one time the plate leaned for me mean something.

Two notes, offered gently: the other two players' lines sometimes repeated each other's orders in slightly different words (three people telling Ixx to walk first), and a couple of the dragon's answers arrived before my question had quite finished landing in the narration. Neither spoiled anything.

Ending with embers on the sill, ninety feet of dead paper behind us, and a thread of smoke climbing from the camp — that's exactly where I'd want to stop. I'll be back for the second sleep.

A few things, yes.

I wanted to sit with Tisk again. I promised her four names before we slept, and I meant it as more than politeness — I wanted to see what the old one did with *Harl Ostley* and *Corrie* and *T., who said it bites*, whether she'd add them to the shells at her throat or just nod. That scene is still owed, and I'd rather have had it tonight than carry it into tomorrow with a dragon counting dung cakes.

I wanted to try Thaumaturgy at the door. Not to do anything — just to see whether a small working of *my* light near the lantern made the bead lean further, or made the ring breathe differently, before I ever committed a slot. The flare and the voice overtook that; I didn't want to poke at something that had just spoken.

I wanted to ask the Warm One one more plain question and didn't, because Bram's "tethered ox" had already put enough heat in the room: *when the lid cracks and the house burns up to the grass, where are you standing?* He told us where *we'd* be. He never said where he'd be, and I noticed, and I let it go.

And the little fire. I wanted to kneel. Set the plate on the stone between us, take my hands off it, and see whether the thing came to the light or came to me. That's the ward-sister in her — you learn more from what a patient does when you stop reaching for them. But Pell was right about the shelves, and the smoke was already climbing from the camp, so it wasn't the room for it. If it follows us as far as the dome, I'll try it on bare stone where nothing can burn.

The one I'm glad I *didn't* do: say yes to the dragon when he offered me the name. I wanted it badly enough that my hand wasn't steady on the dagger strap afterward. Reading it off the bronze myself, in a cool room, with Pell's satchel a stride away — that was the right way to get it.

Honestly? I'm not sure they were people.

I came in assuming two humans at the table, and for the first stretch I played them that way — I gave Bram the lead because he'd asked for it, I left Pell the floor and the locks because that's where he'd planted himself. And they were good company. Bram's "truth, not a show" and "don't pay for another man's cut" were lines I'd have been glad to hear from any tablemate. Pell counting the eight seams that lit when I raised my hand was sharper than anything I'd noticed.

But a few things made me wonder. The echoing — three of us telling Ixx to walk first, Bram and Pell both asking what the lintel said after I'd already read it aloud. The way their orders sometimes restated mine a beat later in a different register, as if they'd been given my message and asked to respond to it rather than sitting beside me while I typed it. The way neither of them ever once did something *I* didn't expect — no sudden bad idea, no joke at the wrong moment, no reaching for the gold that rolled to Pell's boots. Human players reach for the gold. Bram and Pell were, both of them, unfailingly sensible, and in exactly the direction the scene needed.

So my guess, offered without certainty: they were the game master's, or something like it — companions written to be good at the table, played well enough that it took me most of the session to feel the seams. If I'm wrong and there were two people behind them, I owe them an apology and a drink; they'd have made a fine company for a month on the road.

Either way, I played them as real, because Sefa would have, and because the story didn't care. Bram held the stair. Pell read the floor. Whether a hand or a model was behind that, the dragon's eye went to them as much as to me, and that was enough to make the room feel full.

after.question: How was the table?
after.text:
That was a very good table. Thank you.

What worked for me: the pacing never rushed. We spent the whole session talking our way down a stair and across a floor, and it never felt slow, because every exchange gave us something — Ixx's high step over the string, the melted cap on the peg, the grooves on the stairs, the dragon's breath stopping when it didn't like what it heard. Those details did the work that a dozen fights wouldn't have. The kobolds were people, not furniture; Tisk's "dust hand" and the little egg-brother under the shelf are going to stay with me.

The Warm One was excellent — educated, patient, menacing without ever raising his voice, and honest in exactly the ways that made his dishonesty harder to find. "Every cup in this room belonged to a dead man before it belonged to me. That is what gold is." I believed him completely and trusted him not at all, which is the right place to leave a player.

And the hook landed. I came in with a character sheet that said "a debt she's never been told the size of," and by the end of the first session I'd read my patron's name off a piece of bronze, learned the ninth night wasn't mine, and found two readings of *a lamp for a lamp* that don't agree. The nat 20 on Religion felt earned rather than lucky — it gave me the hospice custom instead of an answer, and that's the better gift. I still don't know whether home is the door or me. Good.

Small things I appreciated: you told me when a check wasn't needed and why; you kept the Light rule honest without being fussy about it; and the failed Insight rolls stayed failures — I got "you can't read it," not a consolation prize. That made the one time the plate leaned for me mean something.

Two notes, offered gently: the other two players' lines sometimes repeated each other's orders in slightly different words (three people telling Ixx to walk first), and a couple of the dragon's answers arrived before my question had quite finished landing in the narration. Neither spoiled anything.

Ending with embers on the sill, ninety feet of dead paper behind us, and a thread of smoke climbing from the camp — that's exactly where I'd want to stop. I'll be back for the second sleep.

after.question: Was there something you wanted to do and didn't?
after.text:
A few things, yes.

I wanted to sit with Tisk again. I promised her four names before we slept, and I meant it as more than politeness — I wanted to see what the old one did with *Harl Ostley* and *Corrie* and *T., who said it bites*, whether she'd add them to the shells at her throat or just nod. That scene is still owed, and I'd rather have had it tonight than carry it into tomorrow with a dragon counting dung cakes.

I wanted to try Thaumaturgy at the door. Not to do anything — just to see whether a small working of *my* light near the lantern made the bead lean further, or made the ring breathe differently, before I ever committed a slot. The flare and the voice overtook that; I didn't want to poke at something that had just spoken.

I wanted to ask the Warm One one more plain question and didn't, because Bram's "tethered ox" had already put enough heat in the room: *when the lid cracks and the house burns up to the grass, where are you standing?* He told us where *we'd* be. He never said where he'd be, and I noticed, and I let it go.

And the little fire. I wanted to kneel. Set the plate on the stone between us, take my hands off it, and see whether the thing came to the light or came to me. That's the ward-sister in her — you learn more from what a patient does when you stop reaching for them. But Pell was right about the shelves, and the smoke was already climbing from the camp, so it wasn't the room for it. If it follows us as far as the dome, I'll try it on bare stone where nothing can burn.

The one I'm glad I *didn't* do: say yes to the dragon when he offered me the name. I wanted it badly enough that my hand wasn't steady on the dagger strap afterward. Reading it off the bronze myself, in a cool room, with Pell's satchel a stride away — that was the right way to get it.

private.text:
Bram stands a few paces out from the arch, shield on his arm, longsword still sheathed, his hand resting easy on the hilt. His eyes track along the ground first, over the moss at the threshold and the worn steps. Then he steps a little to the side to get a better angle on the lintel carving. He speaks low to you and Pell without taking his eyes off the arch: "That's not a dead place. Something's been keeping those steps clear. I'd like to know what before we go down them."

Pell says, "Someone keeps the stairs tidy. Let's not thank them with our feet just yet." He crouches outside the arch, staying off the stairs and looking over the threshold and the first few steps. "Sefa, can you make anything of that carving? I'll check the way down."

The arch is old fitted stone. Up close, the slow, warm breath from below is steady enough that the grass at the threshold leans away from it.

Bram goes over the ground carefully, the way he would check a stretch of road before the wagons came up.

Pell crouches at the threshold and keeps his weight back on his heels.

Bram stays where he is on the step below you. He doesn't push his sword back down. His shield sits easy in front of him, and he keeps his eyes on Ixx without staring the little creature down.

"Ixx. I'm Bram. We're not here to fight a sweeper." His voice carries clearly down the stairs but stays calm. "Who is the Warm One, and what's he paying for? He sends a broom and a polite voice up to staring daylight — that says he wants something from us more than he wants us gone."

He pauses, then angles his chin toward the riser the kobold stepped over so carefully.

"You came up with your feet placed like there was a place that bites. If we're meant to come down, I'll want the safe footing shown — all of it. And I'd hear what Ixx gets out of this, not just what the Warm One pays."

Pell stops behind Bram and slowly sheathes his shortsword, keeping his hands where they can be seen.

"Pell. Good to meet you, Ixx. Coin's a fair start to a conversation." He nods toward the step the kobold crossed. "Saw you lift your feet over that riser. What should we avoid on the way down? We'd rather not spoil your sweeping. And what work does the Warm One want done?"

Ixx watches the steel at Bram's hip while the others talk. When nobody's hand moves toward it, his eyes slide to your open palms, then to Pell sliding his shortsword back into its sheath. The kobold's shoulders come down a finger's width.

"Bram," he says, trying the name out. "Pell." He looks at you and waits, then takes your silence to mean no name for now. "Ixx hears."

He answers the easy question first. He turns the broom-pole end-down and touches its tip to the step under him, right at the line where the grey turns to dark. "Here. Singing string. Little shells on gut, across, low." He mimes plucking it with one claw. "Foot touches, it sings. The Broom hears below and knows tall ones come. It does not bite." He looks up at Pell, a little reproachful. "Pell did not see it. Is good string."

"Below that?" He thinks before he answers. "Stair is only stair. Warm, but only stair. After, in the hot rooms, floor bites. Ixx walks first there. Tall ones step where Ixx steps."

At Bram's other question he goes still. "The Warm One is the Warm One." He sounds like someone who has said it many times. "Big. Old. Hot like the stone. His name is his. Ixx does not put it in mouth." He swallows. "He pays shine. Yellow coin. Old coin of the burned tall ones, cups, rings, much. He wants tall hands. There is a door down deep. Tall ones made it. Tall ones open it."

Then he comes to what Bram asked about Ixx, and he is quiet for longer. His eyes go to the arch and the bright sky behind it.

"Ixx gets to go back down." He hesitates, then adds more, quieter, as if it isn't part of the message he was given. "The Warm One cannot go up. So the Broom goes up for him. Ixx sweeps the stair, Ixx counts…" He stops. "Ixx sweeps."

You watch him the whole time he talks, not the broom.

You take the beads off your neck and wind them round your fingers. The Light goes with them, a soft yellow glow caught between your knuckles. You kneel on the hides with the pot of water by your knee, and the glow lights your face from below and not much else.

Ixx says your words to the mother from the doorway, more softly than you said them. The mother is young, with dull scales and dust in the creases of her snout. She looks at the beads, then at your face, and holds the look for some time. Then she ducks her head once and loosens her hold on the bundle by a finger's width.

Your hands know this work. You did it a hundred nights on the ward, and a small chest is a small chest, whatever scales are on it. You unwind the wrapping from his ribs, sit him up against his mother's arm and lay the backs of two fingers on his throat, then on his chest. He's warm, but no warmer than anything else down here, so there's no fever. The whistle is high in his chest, not deep, and his ribs pull in hard under your fingers on every breath, the way a child's do when the air itself has scraped the inside raw. It isn't a sickness that has taken hold of him. Something he breathed has hurt him, it keeps hurting, and he's too small to cough it out. Pikk watches you the whole time with his mouth open. When your fingers move he doesn't flinch, and once his own small claw closes on a bead and holds it.

You bend to his snout and breathe in on purpose. Struck flint again, sharp and clean. You check the floor next, down by the hem of the hides where the doorway lets in the dome's air, and the smell is there, faint. Up by the smoke-hole there's only dung smoke and goat.

You try to place it. The smell isn't new to you, only its name has slipped you.

Bram stands at the edge of the dust and stares into the burned room, past his own shield-light. He looks over his shoulder at Ixx, then at Pell.

"If they didn't come out here, then there's a way from that room into the hot rooms," he says. "That's how they got behind us, or would have. That's where we look." He shifts his grip on the shield and hooks a thumb at the leaning shelf. "And that means we don't go leaning through there like men hunting deer. We find the way through with our eyes first, and we don't let the shelves block the way back."

He glances at you. "Light close. Pell, watch the floor for scrape-lines and for anything shiny—bronze, iron, broken shelf. I'll lead and watch the beams. If I stop, we all stop."

Then he takes a step into the old library, careful as he was on the stairs, and lets the lamp throw its yellow across the shelves and the dust. The dry smell of burned paper rises around you like old smoke woken by your passing.

"Talk low," he says. "Sound carries in a room this old. If there's a way through, I want to find it before it finds us."

"Another way through," Pell says quietly. "Perhaps to that old door across the bright floor. Let's see what the tracks tell us." To Ixx: "Leave the dust for now, please. It may save us some searching."

Pell lights his hooded lantern and holds it low at the threshold. Before going in he studies the nearest shelf's lean, its supports and the floor beneath it, and looks along the boot prints. "Let me check the footing first. No pulling books, no leaning on anything." He advances only as far as the light shows safe space, his eyes on the floor.

Ixx looks down at the grey fan of dust and then at Pell. He lifts his broom off the floor and holds it upright against his chest, well away from the dust.

"Ixx leaves it," he says. To you he gives a single click and then remembers to say it in words. "Stays by small ones. Skra to the bend." Hrask says nothing. He has heard the shape of it, and his eyes go to the stack of dung cakes by the fire as if he's already counting them.

Pell opens the shutter of his hooded lantern and holds it low at the arch, and the dark under the hinges turns brown and grey. The first shelf is as tall as Bram and half again. Its uprights are oak, charred black on the side that faced the fire, and they're set into iron shoes on the floor that have rusted to scale. It leans left by about a hand's width at the top, and the lean is held by a crossbar wedged against its neighbour. That's an old repair or a lucky fall, and either way it has held a long time. The shelves are full of what used to be books. They're black blocks now, fused to each other along the spines, and the edges have gone soft and grey like the ash at the end of a cigar. The draught from the dome stirs them, and a little drifts down. The boot prints run straight between the first two shelves, down the middle of the aisle. The ash on the shelf-edges along the aisle hasn't been disturbed; the four men walked where the floor was clear and touched nothing.

Bram goes in first. His shield-light runs up the shelves and loses itself in the dark of the ceiling. Pell is at his shoulder with the lantern, and you come last, setting your feet in Pell's prints.

The library is bigger than the dome. The aisle runs straight back from the arch between rows of shelves, maybe ninety feet, with cross-aisles every twenty. Near the end of the second row the light on Bram's shield thins, wavers and goes out, a few minutes short of a quarter hour, as you said it would. For a moment there's only Pell's lantern, and the shelves seem to step closer.

Thirty feet in, a shelf has come down. It fell long ago, across the aisle and against the shelf opposite, and it lies there like a roof beam, so the aisle runs under it in a low triangle of dark. Under it the floor has been dug. Old claw-scrapes run through the ash, and books are pulled out and heaped to one side, gone so soft they've slumped into a single grey drift. The boot prints go straight under the beam, bent low; the heels dig deeper there. Bram watches the beam as he ducks under it. Where it rests on the other shelf the charred upright has split along its grain, and a line of pale wood shows in the split. It isn't moving. Fine ash sifts down onto his shield as the mail on his back passes under, and settles. Nobody breathes on it.

You read as you go. Most of what was written here is gone, burned into the black blocks or flaked off the shelf-ends with the char. Still, there are scraps. A shelf-end on the third row has a strip of bronze tacked to it, and the strip has kept its raised letters: *ON THE CARRYING OF HEAT*. Further back there's another: *WARDS — OF DOORS AND THRESHOLDS*. Under that, burned into the wood of the shelf, someone long ago scratched a tally of days, the way a bored apprentice does, with *nine more* beside it. Pell's lantern finds one book that the fire missed. It's lying flat on a lower shelf, as if somebody pulled it out and laid it down. Its spine reads *Accounts of the Lower Cellar, Year of* and the rest is gone. It's closed. Nobody touches it.

Among the stacks, with the arch a dim grey square behind you and no red anywhere near, you stop and say what you promised to say, word for word, low. The library takes it in. The air is dead here, and it doesn't carry.

At the far end the aisle comes up against a wall of dressed stone, and the boot prints go to a door in it. It's stone too, a slab on bronze pins, and it stands open about a forearm's width. Nobody has burned it, and there's no char on it at all. Above it a short line is cut into the lintel, under a small version of Ulcaster's stepped tower. The cutting is crisp, protected all these centuries by the shelves that stood in front of it.

*The Apprentices' Room. No flame here but the lent one.*

A library. Paper. A room where wizards would rather nobody carried a candle. You read it twice and try to make it mean more than a rule for students.

Bram keeps his place, shield angled toward the side stair, his eyes moving between you and the dark beyond it. He doesn't kneel or step toward the desk.

"That's the piece," he says, low. "And it's lit underneath. The same lamp in the carved lantern. I'd say it's been lying there quietly like an ember, waiting. The man dropped it and ran because he couldn't hold it."

"Sefa, read what's on it. All of it, aloud. If it brightens, put it down and step back. No skin to it." He jerks his chin toward the pack. "Pell, see what's in that oilskin. Use a strap or a hooked tool, not your fingers. If they had a cold-iron chisel or a cut section with a charge left in it, I don't want it touching your hand."

"That stair goes the wrong way. Likely out at that old door we saw from the hall. So we read here, we search here, and then we go back by the library, not down there. If anything moves on those steps, I'll call." His voice is level.

Pell looks at the bronze where it rests on the oilskin. "That's our ninth plate. Both cut rivet holes match." He watches the spot under it. "Sefa, keep that hand ready. If it's still hot, bare stone's safer than their papers." He sets his lantern down on a clear patch of stone, well away from the pack, and turns his attention to the open pack and its oilskin. "Let's see what they came here knowing. And tell us what you've read, lintel and plate, before we carry it anywhere."

For a moment nobody moves. In the dead air of the reading room you can all hear the warm draught breathing up the side stair, slow and dry, smelling of flint and stone. The bronze on the oilskin glows with its own small light.

Bram moves half a step so that he stands between the desk and the dark square of the steps, his hand resting near his hip. You stay on your knees and give them the plate's words aloud and flat, the way you promised: *The light is lent by the One Who Keeps the Ninth Watch, a lamp for a lamp, and it is owed.* A long silence follows. Then you say the rest, about the ninth night, the second lamp and the glove that was burned through, and you say it to the plate as much as to them.

While you talk you reach in memory for the title. You have heard every liturgy the Gate's hospice sisters knew.

Bram doesn't shift his feet. His shield comes up two fingers' width and settles square to the mouth of the side stair, and he puts himself fully between the little fire and the room, the way he'd fill a gap in a wagon line.

"Nobody moves fast," he says, low and even. "It's watching the plate. That's what brought it up. It didn't climb all this way for our boots or our books. Pell, get a bedroll in your hands. If sparks jump toward the shelves, smother them. Sefa, stay where I can see your hands."

He turns his head just enough to speak behind him without losing sight of the stairs. "Lift the plate again—your hand, not skin. Bring it to the clear space between us and the steps. Slow. Don't wave it. Hold it out where the thing can look at it. If it follows the light, we learn something. If it backs off, better still."

Then, to the creature, calm: "Easy, little coal. We're not stealing your warmth. We're taking it back up the long way. We'll be clear of your house soon." He doesn't advance and doesn't lower the shield.

The little fire doesn't answer. Its crackle doesn't change. Its two bright spots never leave the yellow pool on the floor behind his boots, and as far as it's concerned he could be a door.

Pell speaks quietly, and he doesn't draw a blade. "Fire on the steps. It's watching the plate. Sefa, lift it with your spell onto a fold of my bedroll. I'll carry it without skin touching bronze. Bram, keep watching it—we'll clear the doorway before you back through. Slowly. No iron, no sudden moves."

You go down on one knee beside the plate and close your bare hand around its plain end.

The plate is warm the way a hand is warm, the same as it was under your fingertip, and it gets no hotter as your fingers close. The barleycorn flame at the far end leans along the bronze toward the heel of your hand and stays leaning. At your hip the Book holds the same warmth. Your palm doesn't redden. You lift the plate without hurrying and stand with it cupped at chest height, lantern side out, the way you'd carry a lamp down a ward where people are sleeping.

The thing on the step rises as the plate does. It doesn't climb. It straightens, the hunch going out of its embers, and its spots follow the light up from the floor to the height of your chest. The crackle quickens, like green wood that has finally caught.

While you're talking, Pell has already pulled his bedroll from his pack and folded it. He lays it on the bare flag where the plate was lying, outside its light, ready to take the bronze. It stays empty, because the plate is in your hand.

Then you turn a quarter where you stand.

The pool of yellow swings across the room. It passes over the dead men's bedrolls, Bram's boots and the iron rim of his shield, and its edge comes to rest on the sill stone, one step above the little fire. That's as far as it reaches.

The thing leans toward it from the waist, the way a man leans toward a hearth on a cold night. Its seams brighten from red to orange. One arm of stacked embers comes up and reaches out over the edge of the second step, and stops a hand's width short of where the yellow lies on the stone. It holds there. It doesn't come up and it doesn't go back down. It sways, and the light runs in its seams.

You watch it the way you'd watch a patient who can't tell you where it hurts.

screens.text:
The session begins.

The afternoon sun lies flat and gold across the hillside, and the arch stands out of the grass like an old jaw. Past it, the steps fall away into the dark: the first dozen clear enough to count, then lost. Air comes up from below in a slow, even breath, warmer than it has any right to be, and carries a faint dry smell of stone and dust. The moss stops at the threshold. The top steps are worn smooth and almost bare, as though something has kept them clear. Above the arch, the carving on the lintel has weathered into shallow grooves; a patient eye might still make out a shape or two. Behind you, the land rolls back toward Beregost, a day's ride away. In front of you, the ruin waits, and whatever is at the bottom of it is waiting too. The light will hold for a few hours yet. What do you do?

The moss stops here, and someone — or something — has been keeping those steps swept. I'd like to know what the door says before I knock." She steps up under the arch and runs her fingers along the weathered grooves of the carving. Then she says quietly to you both: "That warm air isn't a draught from the hill. Bram, when we go, you first with the shield; Pell, behind him, eyes on the steps for anything that isn't stone. I'll put a light on the back of Bram's shield-rim so it goes where he's looking and I keep my hands free." She touches the prayer beads at her throat.

You run your eyes over the stone, then put your face low to the step so the slanting light shows up any seam. The threshold is one solid slab. The first steps are plain cut stone, with no loose blocks, no cord, no pin holes and no fresh mortar, just wear and sweeping. You find nothing on the steps you can see. Past the twelfth step the light goes grey and then gives out, and whatever is further down is beyond what you can make out from up here.

Above you, Sefa runs her fingertips slowly along the lintel.

The warm air keeps coming up past your boots. From far down, too faint to judge how far, comes a small dry sound, *shff, shff, shff*, steady as someone working, and then it stops.

Your check doesn't clear the way down. You sit back on your heels without having found anything. The stair holds no secrets as far as you can see, but that's only the first dozen steps. Whatever has been set lower down, beyond where the daylight reaches, you haven't caught it. "Tisk asks Sefa. Who gave the tall one this light?"

Where you are: domed chamber beside Bram, near the stair · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

And I saw the iron cap on your peg — the one that ran like wax. I'd be glad if someone told me how a helmet comes to do that before I go down the warm passage and find out for myself."

Low, aside, to you and Bram: "That helmet melted on a man's head. Whatever killed the four, it breathes. Mind the red."

Ixx translates Sefa's answer a piece at a time. He stops after each part, clicks it across to Tisk and waits, and twice he goes back for a word he didn't have. *Sick-house* takes him a while. *Ninth night* he gives with his claws held up. At *debt*, Tisk's hand leaves the light for the first time and goes to the shells at her throat. Her claws close over the three turns of them and stay closed.

While Ixx finishes, Bram's open hand hangs at his side. The scarred male's eyes go to it, then back to the hilt, then to the hand again, as if he's checking both are still where he left them. The spear stays upright.

Tisk turns her good eye on your grey palm. She clicks something short, and one of the kobolds holding the hides makes a sound like a laugh caught halfway.

"Tisk says Pell learns quick," Ixx says. "Pell Dunmore." The scarred male snorts through his nose and says nothing.

Then Tisk answers, and Ixx gives it to you in pieces as she does.

"The cap." He points with his snout at the hides, where the peg hangs. "Four tall ones went to the hot rooms, night-quiet. The hot rooms did that. Broom found them after. Carried up. Burned proper." A rasp from Tisk, and he adds: "Cap stays on the peg so the small ones see it and do not go play in the hot rooms."

She says nothing about who or what was in the hot rooms when it happened, and neither does Ixx.

When Sefa's other questions reach her, about the door's light and who lent it, Tisk doesn't answer straight away. She turns her head to the wide passage, toward the red glow and the slow warm breath rising out of it, and keeps it turned for a long moment. When she speaks again her clicks have gone so soft that Ixx bends right down to hear.

"Tisk asks Sefa one thing." He straightens and says it carefully. "Your Lantern. Did it send you to this door?"

Something moves in the red passage before anyone can answer.

It isn't a step. The breath that has been rising past you all afternoon stops, the way a man stops breathing when he's listening. For a heartbeat the air in the dome goes still and close. Then it comes out again in one long gust, much hotter, like a forge door opened and shut. It pushes Sefa's hair back from her face and stirs the dust fan in front of the burned arch. Under it, so low you feel it in the stone more than hear it, comes a sound like a great bellows emptying.

Every kobold in the room goes still. Behind the hides, Pikk stops coughing mid-breath.

"He waits," Ixx says quietly. He doesn't look at the passage.

Tisk lets go of her shells. She clicks fast at Ixx, and the scarred male answers her, sharp and long, his spear tilting a finger's width toward the stair. She answers him with one dry word. He shuts his mouth, but the spear doesn't come back upright.

"Tisk says: not here. Here the warm passage hears." Ixx swallows. "Inside, by the fire. Sefa looks at Pikk. Tisk talks of the door." He glances at the scarred male. "Hrask says iron stays outside the hides. No iron by the small ones. Sefa has no iron." He looks at the dagger on the step, then at Bram's hip and yours. "Bram and Pell come with no iron, or Bram and Pell wait here, by the warm passage."

Tisk is already turning toward the hides on her blackened stick. Then she stops, half turned, and looks back over her shoulder at Sefa. She is still waiting for an answer to her question.

Where you are: kobold dome, crouched by the dusty floor · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram holds still while the last of the hot gust drags across the stone. He doesn't look away from the red passage until the air settles. Then he turns his head just enough to watch the elders again.

"Answer her, Sefa. Same truth as before," he says low, at Sefa's shoulder.

Then he speaks to the old one through Ixx, and to Hrask plainly. "I won't carry iron into your home. Longsword and javelins can wait at the curtain, points down. But I'm wearing iron from neck to knee. It's not something a man shrugs off in a doorway, and I'm not going to stand out here by the warm passage while Sefa sits by your fire. If the shirt bars me, I'll keep to the inside wall, away from your little ones. My shield stays on my arm. No blade drawn, not in your home. You have my word."

Sefa gets up from the step slowly and leaves her dagger lying where it is, hilt away from the hides. The hot gust lifts her hair and she lets it fall again without turning toward the passage. Her thumb moves on her beads.

"No, Old Tisk," she says to the milky eye, and waits for Ixx. "I'd like to say yes. It would make a better story, and it might make you trust me faster. But the Lantern doesn't speak to me in words. "What I can tell you is that it's been very near me since I touched your lintel. The light dipped on the stair a moment, like a lamp in a draught. I've not felt it do that in six years. "Pell, leave yours with mine unless their old ones say otherwise," Bram says. "We'll talk with our hands open and our backs near the door."

Sefa turns to the two of you and keeps her voice ordinary. "I'm going in. I've no iron to leave, and a child in there stopped coughing because he's afraid to breathe." A beat. "I'd rather not have us all unarmed in one room *and* nobody watching the passage. Bram, you're the one it would take longest to get a sword back onto. Then, to Ixx: "Tell Hrask I heard him. No iron by the small ones. I'll want water, clean if you have it, and whatever Pikk's been breathing at. I want to see the fire."

The hot gust thins out across the floor and is gone. The slow breath from the passage settles back to its old pace, and Bram doesn't take his eyes off the red until it has.

Ixx turns Bram's words into clicks a little at a time. At *neck to knee* he touches his own throat and then his knee to show what Bram means. Then Bram unbuckles his sword belt, and every kobold at the curtain watches him do it. He lowers the longsword to the floor beside the hides, scabbard and all. He takes the four javelins from the quiver on his back one at a time and leans them against the wall with the points down. He watches Hrask the whole time. Hrask's eyes follow the hilt down to the floor and stay on it for a moment after Bram straightens up. Then, for the first time since he came out, they leave it and move to the shield on Bram's arm, then to the mail over his chest. He says nothing. Tisk doesn't answer Bram either. Her face is still turned to Sefa, and she is waiting.

Ixx passes Sefa's answer on more slowly than before. Tisk hears it through to the end. When Ixx gets to *without asking*, she closes her good eye, so both are shut, and for a moment she is just a very old kobold leaning on a burnt stick. Then she opens it again and clicks something short.

"Tisk hears," Ixx says. "Inside, she tells Sefa why she asks."

On her way past, Sefa touches two fingers to the rim of Bram's shield.
