Ixx gives Hrask her words about the small ones, then calls her request through the hides. Someone inside answers in a rasp.

You lay your shortsword, both daggers, the unstrung bow and the quiver at the foot of the stair beside Sefa's knife.

Ixx turns from the tall ones to the elders and back, carrying three things at once. Tisk and Hrask go at it quickly. Tisk says one thing, Hrask says a lot, and Tisk says the last word.

"Tisk says shirts come," Ixx says. "Bram's iron shirt. Pell's shirt with little studs. A shirt does not cut. The round wood on Bram's arm comes too." He looks sideways at Hrask. "Hrask says then Hrask stands by Bram. By the door, close, all the time Bram is inside." Hrask has already moved. He stands inside the hides next to the doorpost with his spear upright, and the space he has left beside him is exactly wide enough for a man in mail.

Ixx points a claw at the roll of oiled cloth on your belt. "Pell's little iron stays out. Hrask says small ones take small shiny things, and then Hrask has to go and take them back." One of the kobolds holding the hides open looks down at its feet.

Tisk ducks through the gap, and Sefa follows her in.

Ixx stays in the doorway, half in and half out. He passes on what Sefa asked to see and brings back Tisk's answer.

"Not this fire. This fire is for meat." He tips his snout back over his shoulder, toward the dome and the red beyond it. "The fire Pikk breathes is down the warm passage. When the hot rooms breathe bad, the bad comes up, comes in here. The smoke-hole does not take it."

The dome is dark apart from the red at the end of the passage and the firelight through the gap. Hrask stands at the doorpost with the empty place beside him, and he doesn't move.

Where you are: the dark dome by the stair, outside the hides · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram doesn't cross the threshold. He steps up to the open doorway and takes the space at Hrask's side, his shield angled outward toward the dim red at the end of the passage. He leaves his sword and javelins on the floor just to his left, within a stride, and folds his arms over his chest carefully, so the mail doesn't clatter.

"Then I'll keep the door," he says to Ixx and Hrask. "Your roof, your rules. I can see the passage from here, and I can hear her." He glances once at Hrask. "You don't have to stand close. I don't move from this spot unless I'm called or there's iron in that passage."

Hrask doesn't step back when Bram comes up beside him. Ixx, half in and half out of the hides, passes on *you don't have to stand close*. Hrask hears it out with his eyes on the mail. Then he plants the butt of his spear on the stone a hand's width from Bram's boot and leaves it there. He says something short. Ixx doesn't translate it, and from the look of him it didn't need translating. Then Hrask turns a quarter, so he's standing next to Bram instead of facing him, and looks out the same way Bram does, across the dark dome toward the dull red at the end of the passage.

You lay the roll of oiled cloth beside the weapons. As you say your piece about shiny things, the small kobold holding the hides open looks at the tools on the floor, then quickly up at the ceiling, and tucks both hands behind its back. Hrask doesn't turn his head, but his tail flicks once at the little one, and it goes red to the ear-frills.

You duck under the hides. The vault is low enough near the door that you have to keep your head bent for the first few steps. You find a place by the wall, a little behind and to one side of the fire, close enough to hear Tisk and well clear of the child and the woman holding him. The doorway stays open to your left, with Bram's mail filling half of it.

Reading a room is your trade, so you do it while you wait.

The kobolds along the walls watch you and then, slowly, go back to what they were doing. One is twisting gut into cord. Two are scraping a goat hide pegged out flat on the floor. One is feeding dung cakes to the fire from a basket.

At the back of the warren, where the vault drops lowest, a gap in the stone leads to a second, smaller cellar. Something moves in there, and the smell gives it away before the shapes do: two goats, tethered to a ring in the wall, brown and white, chewing. They're a farmer's goats, not wild ones. One has a neat V-notch cut in its left ear, and that's an owner's mark anywhere on the Sword Coast. Two long poles lean against the wall next to the gap, with crosspieces lashed between them. Their undersides are worn smooth and pale where they've been dragged over stone, many times.

By the door, under the peg with the melted cap, there's a low shelf cut into the wall. On it sits a shallow basket woven from the same peeled twigs as Ixx's broom, and in the basket is what the fire didn't take. There are four belt buckles. Two of them are slumped and run at one edge, like the cap. There's the iron toe-cap of a boot, scorched blue-black. And there are bones: a jaw, some small bones of a hand, part of a long bone from a leg, all of them blackened right through, the way bone goes when it's been in a very hot fire. Someone has laid them out in rows with care, not just dumped them.

Tisk has lowered herself onto a folded hide by the fire. She props the blackened stick across her knees and turns her good eye toward the hearth, where the child is. For a long moment she just watches. Then she clicks something low to Ixx without looking away.

"Tisk says: first Pikk," Ixx says from the doorway, loud enough for the whole room. "Then the door. She waits."

She sits and waits. The child whistles at the end of each breath. Out in the dome the passage breathes in, long and slow.

*(Out of game: no roll was needed. You set your tools down with the weapons, go in after Sefa with your hands in plain view and your head bowed under the vault, and sit by the wall where you don't block Pikk or the doorway.)*

Where you are: inside the kobold warren, by the wall near the fire · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Out at the doorpost Bram stands with his arms folded and his shield angled toward the darkness. He says something low to Ixx that doesn't carry in to you, and Ixx answers just as low. Bram shifts his weight from heel to heel without leaving the doorway, and glances once through the curtain.

Sefa pulls the pot off the fire's edge with the hem of her sleeve and sets it under Pikk's snout, then draws the goat hide up over the mother's head and the child's together. The mother stays still under it like a tent. "Breathe over the water, little one. Slow as you can." Sefa's free hand goes in under the hide's edge, flat on the small heaving chest, and between her knuckles the beads brighten, slowly and steadily, like a lamp wick turned up a notch.

The child's breathing changes. The whistle drops from a thin shriek to a soft wheeze, the sound of a child with a cold, not a child fighting for air. The cough that started a moment ago breaks off. From under the hide the mother makes a small sound. It isn't a word.

"That's not the word that costs," Sefa tells the mother, and Ixx carries it across. "That's just the light. It should take the rawness out of his chest for now. It won't stop the bad air coming in — nothing I carry does that. Only the stair does."

Then she sits back on her heels and answers Tisk, with Ixx carrying it a piece at a time. "My hand, Old Tisk. Everything I've ever done with this light, I chose to do — the Lantern has never moved my fingers for me. If it wants a thing opened, or kept shut, it will have to tell me so plainly, and I'll still decide. But I'll be honest about the other half. I don't know what the debt is. If the thing you said is true — that what is lent, someone comes for — then I may be the one it's come to collect from, and I'd rather find that out standing at your door with my eyes open than have it find me asleep in the Gate."

She raises her voice a little for the next part. "That smell isn't a beast. Every book I've read that stood near dragonfire says smoke, musk, scorched meat. This is clean stone heated past what stone can bear — *called* fire. A bound elemental, a working on the Plane of Fire, something that eats heat. Its fumes are heavy; that's why they come in at the floor and the smoke-hole can't take them." She looks at Tisk. "Your deep door has a lantern that's been going out for a lifetime, and the stair gets warmer every year it fades. I think the lantern on that door is *holding* something, Tisk, and it's running out. And your Warm One has red scales and can't climb his own stair, and wants tall hands to open it."

Quietly: "So before I go down there I want to know two things. Does the Warm One know the flame is dying? And does he want the door opened to let something *out* — or to get *in* before the light goes?"

Tisk listens with her good eye on Sefa's face. At *I may be the one it's come to collect from*, the old kobold's head tilts a little to one side, the way a bird's does. When the whole answer is across, she lets out a long dry click.

"Tisk hears. Sefa's hand." Ixx straightens. "Sefa says the true thing and the bad thing together. Tisk likes this more than only the true thing."

She answers the questions one at a time. "Does he know the flame dies." Tisk lays a claw against her milky eye, then her good one. "He knows. He lies by the door. When the flame was big he did not look at it. Now he looks every sleep. Long."

The second takes her longer. She looks into the dung fire and clicks so softly that Ixx bends nearly to her snout. "Under the door is the fire-not-fire. It wants nothing. Fire only eats." Ixx swallows. "The Warm One is not under the door. The Warm One wants up." Tisk draws a line in the air with one claw, from the floor up toward the vault. "When Tisk already had eggs, the Warm One came down the stair. Small. Like a goat. Hungry. He followed the warm." She lowers the claw. "Down is easy." She stops there, and from the way her jaw sets she means to.

Sefa gets up slowly and lifts the beads so the mother can see she's taking the glow with her. "Keep the hide on them till the water cools. Then up to the bend, all the small ones, whenever the floor breathes like that. Pell — I think we go and hear him. But if he lies to me about that smell, I'll know it, and we walk back up."

Sefa doesn't need your flasks, so nobody takes one. Pikk's mother has her head out from under the hide now, though. Her eyes go to the flasks and rest there a moment, the way the little door-holder's went to the tools. Then she looks at you, sitting still against the wall, and her eyes stay on you a little longer than they did before.

Out in the dome the passage breathes in.

Claws on stone, fast. Skra comes through the gap in the hides at a run, her sling wound tight on her wrist, and a rasp from Hrask outside follows her in. Sefa's light falls on her heaving sides. She stops in the middle of the warren and speaks to the room, high and quick, and every kobold along the walls goes still again.

Ixx doesn't want to translate it. He looks at Tisk, and Tisk lifts her chin a finger's width.

"Skra brings his word," Ixx says. "The Warm One says…" His tail is around his ankle again. "'The tall ones talk long with the small ones. I am not small. The tall ones come now, or the tall ones go up, and the Broom goes with them.'" He stops. Skra rasps one more thing, and he adds, very quietly: "Skra says his breath was very hot when he said it."

Tisk doesn't move. Skra stands panting in the light and stares at the beads in Sefa's fingers, then at Sefa, waiting to see which of the tall ones answers.

Where you are: inside the warren, sitting against the wall · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram speaks to Skra without raising his voice, so the whole warren hears him. "The Warm One wants us, he gets us. But we don't come down there running, with the Broom between us and his temper." He shifts his shield on his arm and steps back from the doorpost. "We'll go down in his time—now—but we go on our feet, not his summons." Then he raises his chin toward Tisk. "Old Tisk, we won't leave Pikk worse and we won't drag the Broom into a fight." He jerks his head toward the red passage. "Hrask and Skra brought us here; Ixx kept us alive on the stair. Skra hears Bram out with her sides still heaving, then turns her snout to Ixx. He passes Bram's words on in clicks. He says them more quietly than Bram did and takes no longer over it than he has to.

Bram bends for his gear. He takes his time, and the kobolds watch all of it. The sword belt goes round his hips and the longsword stays in its scabbard. The javelin quiver goes across his back, and his mail chimes once, low. Hrask watches the hilt go back on his hip, then looks at Bram's face.

Ixx carries Bram's words to Tisk. The old one hears them to the end and answers in a few slow clicks.

"Tisk says: Bram says *not worse*. Tisk hears." Ixx looks to Hrask, because the rest was meant for him.

Hrask answers Bram himself, in one long rasp, without looking at the passage. He keeps his spear upright, and when he's done he plants its butt back on the stone by the doorpost, where it was before.

Ixx gives Skra Sefa's message a piece at a time: *slow, talking… a sick child… his door was not going anywhere.* Skra's eyes go to the beads one last time. Sefa holds up her grey palm, and Tisk looks at it for a long moment. Then the old kobold leans forward on her blackened stick and presses her own dusty palm against it, flat, scale to skin. "Tisk says: Sefa's hand, Sefa's promise. Tisk remembers both." Ixx listens to more, and his tail goes round his ankle. "Tisk says one thing for the hot rooms. In the hot rooms, little fires walk. Out in the dome, Sefa takes her dagger off the bottom step and sheathes it. While Bram buckles up, she speaks low to the two of you: "Here's what I've got. You pick up your things one at a time: the shortsword, both daggers, the bow and the quiver. The roll of oiled cloth goes back on your belt, and you check it with your thumb as it goes. Nothing's missing. The small door-holder watches from the gap in the hides with its hands still behind its back.

Sefa turns to the doorway, where Ixx stands half in and half out. "Ixx. Will you walk us down? If it's too much to ask, say so, and we'll follow Skra instead."

She lays two fingers on the inside of Bram's shield rim, and this time the Light wakes full. Ixx has his broom back. He comes out of the hides and stops in front of the three of you. He looks up at Bram, then at Sefa, then at you, in the order you asked him.

He moves to Bram's left side, half a step behind his elbow, where the shield will be between him and the passage. "Ixx walks here. Bram walks first. In the hot rooms the broom says where. Bram's foot, Ixx's broom. Pell's foot, Bram's foot. Sefa last."

Bram faces the passage. "I'll take the red walk first. Let's see what's so old he can't climb his own stair." He says it plainly, and the dome is quiet, so it carries. The breath coming up the passage stops for a moment. Then it comes out again at its old pace, a little warmer.

Ixx doesn't look at the passage, and he says nothing about it.

---

The red passage runs straight and slopes down. It's wide enough that the shield-light doesn't reach both walls at once. Within fifty feet it's hot enough that sweat runs down inside your collar and stays there. The walls were dressed stone once. Along both sides, at waist height, runs a channel cut into the rock and lined with bronze. The metal has gone green-black, and every so often it's pierced with a row of little holes, like a flute. Warm air whispers out of some of them. At one place the bronze has split along a seam, and the stone around the split is glazed and shiny, like the inside of a kiln.

The struck-flint smell gets stronger with every step, and now it clings to the back of your throat.

After about two hundred feet the passage levels out and opens up, and Ixx stops with his broom held across Bram's knees.

"Hot rooms," he says.

It's a long hall, perhaps eighty feet to the far end, with square pillars down the middle holding up a low flat roof. The floor is laid in big flagstones, each about a stride across. Between them are gaps a finger wide, and under the gaps is a red light, as if the whole floor had been laid over coals. Most of the cracks just glow. Some of them breathe. As you watch, a line of cracks to the right of the pillars flushes bright orange and lets out a sigh of heat that blurs the air above it, with a scatter of sparks. Then it dims again. The left side of the hall is quieter, and the stones there are paler and less scorched. The swept path runs that way, a line of clean stones zigzagging between darker ones. Near the middle of the hall, off the path, a patch of flagstones has been blackened in a long smear, as though something burned there and was dragged away. Two shallow grooves run from it back toward the passage.

At the far end of the hall is an arch, and the light beyond it is a deeper red, slow and steady, like the passage's breath made visible.

Something moves in the cracks on the right.

You and Bram both catch it at the same moment. A thin crack between two of the breathing stones brightens, and something stands up out of it. It's knee-high and shaped like a man, a small hunched figure of embers with light running in its seams. It has no face, only two brighter spots where a face would be. It stays there, upright in the heat-shimmer about forty feet off, with the brighter spots turned toward the shield-light. Then it folds back down into the crack. The glow sinks with it, and the stones go dull.

Ixx's tail is round his ankle. He says nothing about the little fire. He sets the bristle end of his broom on the first clean stone of the swept path, just past Bram's left boot.

"Here," he says. "Then the broom says next."

Where you are: edge of the hot rooms, behind Bram · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram doesn't flinch when the little fire stands up out of the floor. He keeps his eyes on it, steady.

"Right side is where the floor's breathing hardest," he says low. "We stay left on the swept path, tight to Ixx. Don't watch the bright cracks. Watch where the next clean stone is." His voice is steady, though it sounds like it costs him some effort.

He sets his boot exactly where the broom's bristles touch, then gives Ixx a nod. "Your floor, Ixx. Show us the next stone. And if one of those little fires comes out close, don't put yourself between it and me."

Sefa stops at the mouth of the hall, her eyes following the bronze channels, the glazed seam, and the long black smear off the path with its two grooves running back toward the passage. She speaks low, just to you, Bram and Ixx: "Those channels aren't a dragon's work. Someone *built* this to carry heat. Bronze pipes, vents, a floor laid over coals. Ulcaster's people, or whoever came after. The hot rooms were a working before they were a lair." She looks at the smear. "And that's where the four died. Off the path, by the bright cracks. Then dragged out. Those are the grooves we saw on the stair."

She breathes in the flint-sharp air and grimaces. "Tisk said little fires walk here, small as Pikk's mother, and they know the Broom but may not know us. If something small and bright comes toward you, Bram, don't swing. Step back onto a clean stone and let it pass. No iron in the red cracks, nothing stopped over them. Ixx's broom, then your foot, then Pell's, then mine, exactly." To Ixx, gently: "You're doing well. Say the stone before Bram steps, not after." Then she falls in last behind you, hem gathered up out of the heat.

Ixx doesn't look at the place where the little fire went down. At Bram's words he moves the broom one stone forward and sets the bristles down.

"Ixx is not between," he says. "Ixx is behind." He thinks about it for a moment. "Behind is good."

Then the crossing starts, a stone at a time. Ixx calls each stone before Bram steps on it, the way Sefa asked. "Here." The broom touches down, Bram's boot follows, then yours, then Sefa's, each on the stone the last one just left. "Here." The path zigzags across the pale left side of the hall. Sometimes it runs two stones straight ahead, sometimes one stone sideways toward the wall. The flagstones are hot through your soles. The air above the cracks shimmers, and every breath of it scrapes your throat.

About a third of the way across, Ixx says "Wait" instead of "Here."

Bram stops. Two stones ahead of him, where the path crosses a seam running out from the right side, the seam goes orange from one end to the other. It lets out a sigh of heat that pushes against your face and throws sparks up past Bram's shield rim. Then it dulls back to red. Ixx counts something under his breath in his own tongue.

"Now. Fast. Here, here."

The broom taps twice and you all cross the seam in two strides each, Sefa last. Behind her the seam is just a red line again.

You see the second one first, and you say so before your next step. A crack off the path to the right, behind Sefa and well beyond the back of the light, brightens. Another little fire stands up out of it, knee-high, embers stacked into the shape of a hunched man. Out on the right side, about where the first one sank, the first one stands up again. Neither comes onto the path. They keep pace with the company stone by stone, each on its own line of cracks, staying out where Sefa's light gives way to red. When Sefa stops, the one behind her stops. When she steps, it steps. Once it drifts closer to her and stops where the shield light thins to dim, and goes no further. It sways there, its two bright spots turned on her.

Ixx sees it too. Without a word he lifts the broom off the floor and tucks the whole bristle end behind his back, pole and all, the way a man tucks a full purse behind him in a crowd.

"They like broom," he says, very quietly. "Ixx likes broom more."

Halfway across, the path brings you level with the long black smear Sefa pointed out from the mouth of the hall. Up close, the blackening is worst at one end and thins out toward the other, and the twin grooves start at the thin end and run back toward the passage. Past the dark end, about fifteen feet off the path, a short bar of dark iron stands upright in a crack. It's as long as a man's forearm, with a flattened head like a mason's chisel, driven or wedged in hard. The crack around it is the brightest on that side of the hall, white-orange rather than red, and the bottom half of the bar has gone cherry-red with heat. The little fire on the right sank back into the floor a few stones from it.

Ixx won't look at the bar. "Here," he says, and the path bends away from it toward the wall.

The rest of the way is the same work: the broom taps, a boot comes down, Ixx says "wait" once more and you wait. As the far end comes closer, both little fires fold down into their cracks, first the one on the right and then the one behind Sefa, and the floor goes back to being just a floor over coals. Ixx brings out his broom again and checks the bristles with one claw. None of them are scorched.

The arch at the far end is broad and low, built of the same dressed stone. Beyond it, the deep, steady red light swells and fades with the breath that has come past you all afternoon. Here it's so close that you feel each draw as a faint pull on your clothes and each letting-go as heat on your face. Ixx stops one stone short of the arch, behind Bram's elbow, his tail wrapped round his ankle.

The breath stops.

Then a voice comes out of the red, deep and slow, in good, old-fashioned Common.

"The one who wonders what is so old it cannot climb its own stair." It pauses, and in the pause the heat leans on you. "Come and see, then, little shield. And bring the lamp nearer. I want to look at it."

Where you are: far end of the hot hall, one stone short of the low arch · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram doesn't answer the voice right away. He rolls his shoulders once under the mail and glances back at Ixx, then at Sefa and you.

"Steady," he says quietly. "It's older than it is subtle. It heard every word we said on the stair. We give it truth, not a show."

Then he steps through the arch with his shield up, the shield-light spreading before him, not crowding the threshold. His sword hand stays easy at his belt, away from the hilt.

"I'm Bram Halloway." His voice carries clear through the heat. "We came down your stair talking, not with night-quiet and iron. The lamp's not mine to offer—she who holds it speaks for it. But it's here." He stops a stride inside. "You asked us to come see. We're here. Now I'll ask what you wanted us to see—the door, or you. And what you'd have us do about either."

The room beyond is big, the biggest thing you've seen under the hill. It's round, about sixty feet across, with a dome high enough to lose the shield-light in. The floor is dressed stone and it's whole here, with no cracks between the flags. It's hot, steady and dry, the way the air over a hearth is hot. The arch is worn smooth on both sides at the height of a horse's shoulder, polished pale. Something big has rubbed past it many times.

The red light comes from the far wall, from a ring.

A channel runs around a round slab set into the wall, about twelve feet across. It's a door made of pale stone, banded with bronze gone black. The channel glows the same coal-red as the cracks in the hot rooms, and it breathes. Above the door the tower is cut into the stone, Ulcaster's stepped crown, sharper than the one on the lintel. In the middle of the slab is the lantern, hooded, with a ring for a handle, the same as at the mouth. In its heart, where the carving would hold a flame, a small light burns. It is lamp-yellow and no bigger than one of Sefa's beads. It doesn't flicker. On the bronze rim, low on the left, a bright scar shows where something has been cut away, leaving pale stone under the black.

Between the arch and the door lies the Warm One.

The dragon lies along the floor in a long curve, with his tail toward the right-hand wall and well clear of the arch. His body is as thick as a loaded cart and longer than a wagon with its team. Under him there's a bed of metal: coins, the rim of a cup, a bent candlestick, old gold pressed flat under his weight. His head rests on his crossed forelegs a few strides from the door, turned toward that small yellow flame, and it's the size of a rain barrel. His wings are folded tight along his back. Their edges are ragged and dull, rubbed thin, the way a sail goes when it's been stowed wet too long. The scales are the deep red of a forge coal, but they're dusty and dry, gone pale round the nostrils and along the jaw. His flanks rise slowly.

The head lifts and turns. The eyes are pale gold. They go first to the shield-light and stay there for a long moment. Then, without the head moving, they slide past it to the yellow bead in the door, and they stay on that even longer. Then they come back to Bram.

"Bram Halloway." He says the name the way a man turns a coin over to read its date. "*Truth, not a show.* You said that at my threshold, as if the stone between us were deaf." His breath stops. In the stillness the heat presses on all of you, on the face and the chest. Then it comes out again, slow and warmer. "Then have it. You wondered what is so old it cannot climb its own stair. I am not old, little man. I have had twenty winters in this house. I came down that stair on my own feet when I was smaller than your shield. I stay because what I want is here."

His snout tips a hand's width toward the door.

"That is what I wanted you to see. Your wizards shut it, and their light keeps it shut, and their light is going out. You have eyes. What I would have you do about it I will tell you when I know what you are worth."

Sefa comes to Bram's shoulder and stops in the arch itself, under its worn stones, beside the shield, not past it. She keeps the light on the rim. Her voice is the ward voice, unhurried, pitched to carry into the red without rising: "The lamp stays where it is. It's lighting the floor, and I've been told not to stop over the cracks. You can look at it from there as well as I can look at you. I'm Sefa Marrin. Bram you've heard. The quiet one is Pell. We came down talking, as your kobold asked us to, and we tended a child on the way, because he was coughing on what comes up out of your floor." A beat. "Which is not your breath. I know what dragonfire smells like from the books, and this isn't it. This is called fire — a working. So before you tell me anything, I'd like to hear you say that much true, and then I'll believe the rest of it more easily."

She tips her head back toward the hall without looking away. "And there's an iron bar standing in the brightest crack out there, by the place the four died. Tisk's people won't look at it. I'd like to know who put it in — them, or you."

Then, low, barely moving her lips, to Bram and you: "He speaks like someone who learned Common from a book, not a kobold. Educated. Let him come to the arch; we don't cross it till we've seen the shape of him." Her hand rests on the Book of Shadows at her belt, and her thumb finds the beads at her throat.

The gold eyes move to her at *the lamp stays where it is*, and the pause after it is long.

"Then I will look from here." He does, and not at the lamp. He looks past it at the door again, and then at her. "*Called fire. A working.* You read well, for a sick-house girl." A low sound moves through the floor. It could be amusement. "Yes. That is the house you smell, not me. If you ever smell my breath, you will not be standing to discuss it."

At the iron bar the long head settles back onto the forelegs.

"Your kind put it there. Four of them, by night, with cold iron, cutting at the house's veins to get at my door. The house answered them." The eyes half close. "Had I answered them, the Broom would have found nothing to carry up."

Behind you, Ixx stops at the arch and sets his broom-tip on the first flag inside.

"Here floor is floor," he whispers. "Not near the ring. Not near the shine." Then he stays exactly where he is, one stone back, with his tail round his ankle.

You step through after Bram's boots, keeping your hands clear, and you pick a place the way you would pick a spot in a room full of people you don't trust. Just inside the arch on the left, the wall curves out into a stub of old pillar. Standing there, you have stone at your back and the arch within two strides, and you're the farthest point in the room from the tail. There's room in that space for three, close together. From there you can see the head, the door and the way out, all at once.

"Pell Dunmore," the Warm One repeats, without looking at you. "The quiet one, who came to *hear about my door*." The gold eyes stay on Bram. "Well. You came down talking. Talk. What does the man with the shield want for the use of his hands?"

*(Out of game: Bram is one stride inside the chamber, and Sefa stands in the arch beside his shield, not yet over the threshold. No dice were needed this round.)*

Where you are: by the pillar stub just inside the arch, left side · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram meets the gold eyes and doesn't step any closer.

"My hands aren't for sale until I know what they're buying." His voice stays level. "You've shown me a door and a failing light. That's a problem, not a bargain."

He plants the shield a little more solidly against the heat.

"What I want, in order:

"First, I want the Broom out of this without your heel on them. Ixx brought us down in daylight with straight answers, and your own word got flung at them because we stopped to tend a sick child. I don't work for anyone who treats good service with a threat. So I'll have that said plainly: they stay, and we don't find them worse after we leave.

"Second, I'll want to know what's behind that door, as true as you know it. Not the name, if you don't have it. But what it is, what it does when it's open, and whether the thing that's failing is meant to hold it or let it loose. Because I read the floor too. That heat under the cracks is no natural coal. It'll bite, and it'll take the one who steps wrong.

"Third, my price. You can think on that while I look at the door and hear the rest of what you know. I don't work on a 'may it be enough' promise, and I don't open old seals for old gold alone.

"Last, I want this company to have free passage back up the stair while I think, with our own feet and our own steel, and no clever floor between us and the sky."

He pauses, then adds, not unkindly: "You want hands that won't fail you at the wrong moment. That means you want the one that asks all this. We came down talking. Let's keep doing it."

Sefa keeps her hand on the Book and her eyes on the gold ones. She doesn't step over the threshold.

"Bram will tell you what he wants for his hands. I'll tell you what mine cost, and it isn't gold. You've answered me straight twice — about the fire, and about the four. So I'll ask the third thing straight. You came down a stair smaller than a shield, following the warm, twenty winters ago. You've grown to fill the house. Now you lie here watching the wizards' light die on that door, and you say *what I want is here*." A beat. "What's behind it? Not 'the fire-not-fire' — Tisk gave me that much. What do you think is on the other side that's worth twenty years on a bed of other men's cups, and what do you become when it opens?"

Her thumb moves on her beads. "Because here's what I see from the arch. The lintel upstairs says *by lent light*. That flame in the lantern is the same colour as the one in my hands, and it's been going out all Tisk's life, and the floor breathes hotter every year it fades. That isn't a lock, Warm One. That's a *lid*. Somebody lent a light to hold a fire down, and the loan is running out. If that door opens, I don't think what comes through is a way up for you. I think it's the house, getting out."

She tips her head at the bronze rim, low on the left, where pale stone shows through the black. "And someone has already cut a piece off it. Was that the four, or was that you, in a year when you were less patient?"

Low, to you and Bram, barely moving her lips: "He hasn't said what the door *does*. He's said what he wants. Don't promise hands until he tells us which way it opens."

The Warm One hears Bram's list to the end without moving. When Bram says *threat*, the gold eyes narrow, and they stay narrowed until he has finished.

"In order, then, since you like it that way."

"The Broom. I said they would go up with you, and so they would. A broom goes where it is carried." The sound that moves through the floor might be a laugh. "I do not break my own brooms, Bram Halloway. Who would sweep? Have it plainly, then. They stay. When you go, you will find them as you found them, sweeping."

Behind Bram's elbow, Ixx's tail tightens once around his ankle.

"Your passage. Go up whenever you please." The great head doesn't move. "Nobody going up that stair has ever been stopped."

Then Sefa speaks, and he turns his eyes to her. At *a bed of other men's cups* his breath stops. The heat leans on all of you and keeps leaning, longer than it has before, until it presses on the chest like a hand. Along his flank the tail shifts on the hoard, and a slide of old coin runs off the bed and rings across the stone. Then he breathes out, slow and warmer.

"*Other men's cups.*" He gives it back to her softly. "Every cup in this room belonged to a dead man before it belonged to me, sick-house girl. That is what gold is."

"What lies behind it. The fire your wizards caught and could never put down, and the thing they caught it with: a book bound in iron. The four talked about it on my floor, loudly, as though I were furniture. They wanted the book. I have no use for paper." The eyes half close. "And what do I become? What I am."

"A lid. Yes. You read well." For a moment he is quiet. "Think what happens under a lid that is lifted. The fire rushes out, burns, and when it has nothing left to eat it is less than it was. His snout tips toward the pale scar on the bronze rim.

"The four did that. They had a cold-iron tool and a thief's patience. They cut at the rim, and I let them, because I wanted to see what the door would do." The gold eyes go to the yellow bead in the lantern. "The light jumped when the iron bit. They ran as though it had bitten them back, and they took the piece with them. He turns to the pillar, and to you.

"Opened, little lock. Not mended. You mend what you mean to keep."

The long head comes up off the forelegs then, high enough that the shield-light finally reaches his throat. The scales there are as dull as old brick.

"My price, then, since you asked for yours in order. Open it, and each of you takes from this bed as much as you can carry in two arms, and the iron book goes with you." His breath stops again, briefly. "But tall ones have shown me their backs before. So one of you stays here beside me while the other two go and find what was cut from my door."

The gold eyes come back to Bram and stay on him.

"The man with the shield. At the mouth of my passage you said *I'll take the red walk first.* You are the one who stands where the trouble will come. So come and stand here."

*(Out of game: nobody needed a die. All three of you asked your questions aloud, and he answered them. Whether he told the truth is something the story will show.)*

Where you are: by the pillar in the hoard chamber · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram doesn't move from his one stride inside the room, but he doesn't flinch either. The shield stays up, the lamp-light throwing his shadow long toward the sealed door.

"Here's my difficulty," he says after the dragon's last word. "You want me to stand where the trouble will come, off the path, beside a lid that's been cracking for years, while the other two go looking for a piece of cold iron and a book. He shakes his head slowly, the mail shifting.

Sefa lets the coin finish ringing across the floor before she speaks. She hasn't moved off the threshold, and her hand hasn't left the Book.

"No hostage. Not Bram, not Pell, not me." She says it quietly, without heat. Behind Bram's leg, Ixx's tail is wound twice around his ankle.

The lane lies open in front of Sefa, and she's still on the threshold.

Where you are: by the pillar inside the dragon's chamber · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

She walks the lane slowly, hands open and a little away from her sides, his head and then his neck lying along her left the whole way. Two paces short of the slab she stops in the red breath of the ring and stands a long while looking at the door, without touching it.

You are at the pillar, forty-odd feet from the door, and you read the rim the way you would read a strongbox from across a counting-room. The outer band isn't one piece. In the ring-glow you can count the seams where cast plates meet, each about a hand long, pinned at the joins by bronze rivets with their heads ground flush. You count nine of them around the circle.

Sefa looks at the flame in the carved lantern, a steady bead of yellow. She lifts her right hand and turns the palm toward it, a hand's width short of the stone, and says nothing.

The flame leans toward her palm, the way a candle leans toward an opened door. For the length of a breath it is bigger than a bead. The coal-red ring around the slab misses a breath and stays dull where it should brighten, then comes back. As the flame leans, a hairline of yellow runs along every seam at once, like light under a row of doors, and is gone. It runs along eight seams. At the ninth place, low on the left, there is no plate to run behind. There's only the bright cut and pale stone, and a thin channel in the stone where the plate sat, red as the ring. You have seen this shape before, on a treasury lock in the Upper City: a ward ring with a plate drawn. Somebody cut that plate out between its two rivets, carefully, along the seam, and they knew what they were doing right up to the moment they ran.

You sweep the floor from the pillar back to the arch. The stone is whole and swept by the dragon's own bulk. Coins have scattered where the tail dragged, the candlestick lies by your boot, and you can see the polished stone where something huge has turned around ten thousand times. There's no brass on it, no plate, no scuff of boots running. Whatever the four carried out of here, they didn't drop it in this room.

The Warm One's breath stops again. The sound that comes through the floor this time isn't amusement.

He lifts his head off the stone and keeps it low, level with Sefa and very close to her.

"It knows you," he says. He says it softly, and he means it. "Twenty winters I have lain here, and it has never once leaned for me."

He lets that sit.

"You read the gap, sick-house girl. I read the band before the little thieves cut it. I read it every sleep for twenty winters, until I could say it with my eyes shut. I know what stood there." The gold eye is a stride from her face. "The name your Lantern was called by the ones who borrowed from it, long before it came to a dark ward. And what they promised it, the size of the lending, which is the size of what you owe. Open my door, and I will give you both."

The flame in the lantern flares.

It lights Bram at the arch, and you at your pillar, and Ixx pressed flat behind Bram's boot with his snout on the stone. For an instant the whole room is lit in white-gold.

Then the flame is a bead again. The ring breathes red. The Warm One hasn't moved, and his eye hasn't left Sefa's face.

"Well?" he says.

She tips her head at the outer band without touching it. "And I'll tell you what *I* read that you've never said in twenty winters of reading it with your eyes shut. *Come in who will. She turns side-on to the door, not giving it her back, and raises her voice enough to carry down the lane.

"Bram. Pell. The band says the house of Ulcaster shut this cellar *by lent light*, the year the towers burned. The light was lent by — and there the piece is cut — and it is owed. As she comes level with Bram, she says gently to Ixx, still flat behind Bram's boot: "Tisk's people know every clean stone between here and the stair. When we go back across, I want someone who knows which cracks a dropped bit of bronze would have fallen near — and which ones it would have fallen *into*."

And to the dragon, over her shoulder, without stopping: "You'll have your answer. It's *not yet.* If that's not good enough for a thing that's waited twenty winters, say so now, while I'm still on your floor and you can still see my hands."

The light shrinks back to a bead. For a moment after it does, nobody in the room moves except Bram, who takes one pace into the chamber, clear of the lane, his shield a few inches higher than it was.

The Warm One doesn't look at him. The gold eye stays on Sefa, two paces from his door. When Bram's words reach him (*sugar lump*, *mousetrap*, *killed half the room*) his breath stops and stays stopped, and the heat gathers around them.

As Sefa starts back along the lane, with fifteen strides of his jaw on her left, the long head turns to follow her. It comes no closer. It only turns, the way a cat's head turns after a moth.

When he breathes out at last, it is slow, and hotter than anything yet. The coins under his foreleg tick in it.

"That was not mine." He says it to Bram, without moving his eyes off Sefa. "Twenty winters that light has not answered me. You saw what it did for her. Do not tell me I made it." He lets a pause go by. "*Prove you want it opened slow.* I have lain here twenty winters, Bram Halloway. Show me a slower man than that."

Sefa is a third of the way down the lane. He speaks to her now, low enough that the stone under your boots carries it more than the air does.

"*Never sent a kobold.*" He gives the words back to her almost gently. "Ask the one behind your shield-man how many times my floor was swept for it, sick-house girl. Ask him how many times the stair was swept, and the hot rooms, and the passage, crack by crack. Ask him what they found." The eye half closes. "You read stone better than you read me."

She is halfway now, level with the hinge of his jaw. With her in reach of it, he takes the other thing she said and turns it in front of her.

"*Nothing of the flame goes out.* You say it as though it frightened you." The heat leans on her again. "Then think what it promises. If nothing of the flame goes out, what do you fear from an open door? The fire stays where your wizards put it. It says so in bronze. You read it to me yourself."

He doesn't say what he is.

When you speak of plates and rivets and the burned room upstairs, the head moves away from Sefa for the first time. It's only a hand's width, toward you.

"The burned room." He tastes the words. "Your four went in there by night with their lamps before they came to me. My brooms do not go in." Amusement comes up through the floor, faint and not kind. "They are small, and they are afraid of old paper. Go and look, little lock. Look anywhere you like."

Sefa reaches the end of the lane. Her dagger is still on the threshold stone at Bram's boot. Ixx is still flat behind that boot with his snout on the floor and his tail wound twice round his ankle. As she comes level he turns his head toward her without lifting it, and his mouth moves, too faintly for you to make out anything.

The Warm One lowers his jaw onto his forelegs again, facing the door, as though none of you had ever come in.

"*Not yet,*" he says to the yellow bead. "I have had *not yet* from that door every sleep for twenty winters. I can hear it once more from you." He doesn't raise his voice. "Go and find my piece. Take the sweeper. Read your name off it with your own eyes, since you would rather owe me nothing. But it is a piece of *my* door, and it comes back to this room in your hands. If I hear it go up my stair instead…" A slide of old coin runs off the bed and rings across the stone, without hurry. "…then I will not need sweepers anymore, and the Broom will learn what I do with things I do not need."

His breath goes out, long and even, and the ruin breathes with it.

"One sleep. Not two."

Sefa is back at the arch beside Bram.

Where you are: the dragon's chamber, by the pillar near the arch · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram doesn't pick up the dagger. He lets it lie on the threshold stone beside his boot and speaks to Sefa without taking his eyes off the dragon's head: "Take it up. We don't leave iron on his floor."

Then his voice goes out flat across the chamber, not loud, but meant to carry to every wall: "One sleep. We'll use it." Sefa stoops for her dagger and buckles it on. Her fingers fumble the strap once before they get it. Then she speaks to the dragon's turned head, level:

She turns to the arch and doesn't look at the hoard. "Pell, you've got it. She crouches by the kobold flat behind Bram's boot and keeps her voice for him: "Ixx. Up. You swept every crack for that piece and found nothing, and I was unfair to you about it. Sefa straightens and speaks quietly, side-on to you and Bram: "What the flame said, I'll give you word for word once we're past the string, where only the stair hears. It's short. The Warm One doesn't lift his jaw from his forelegs. His eye stays on the yellow bead in the door.

"Then do not hand it to me," he says when Bram is done. He says nothing at all to Sefa's admission. His breath stops for a moment while she speaks, then comes out again at its old pace, no warmer. From him, that may be the answer.

Ixx gets up off the floor. He picks up his broom and checks the bristles with one claw, then looks up at Sefa crouched beside him. He seems to have expected a kick more than an apology. "Sefa was not unfair," he says, very low. "Sefa did not know." He takes his place behind Bram's left elbow.

At the arch the lamp-yellow light on Bram's shield rim spreads across the first pale stones, and the red of the cracks lies beyond it.

"Here," Ixx says, and the broom touches down.

You go back the way you came, one stone at a time. Bram, in front, speaks low to Ixx: "On your feet, sweeper. Show us the clean stones going back. All of us step where you step." A beat. "And tell me how many times you've swept this path for that plate — crack by crack. I'd like to know what I'm looking at before I go groping into a seam that breathes fire."

Ixx answers him between stones, in pieces, and he never calls the next stone late.

"How many sweeps." *Here.* "Every sleep, from the sleep the four died. Ten." *Here.* "All Broom. Big ones, small ones. Every crack on the pale side, with claws, with sticks." *Wait.* A seam to the right goes orange and sighs, and sparks drift past the shield rim. "Now. Here, here." On the far side he goes on. "The bright side, not. Bright side, little fires walk. Broom sweeps up to the bright, not in." He thinks about it. "If the piece went in a bright crack, it is gone. Bronze goes soft in the bright. Bram's head turns toward it. Then the little fire folds down into its crack, and that side of the hall goes dark again.

Ixx has seen where Bram's head turned. "Old door," he says, before Bram can ask. "Tall ones' door. Floor bites there, all the way." His tail goes round his ankle. "Broom does not go."

He sees four come back up out of the red and lets out a breath through his nose that might be relief.

Ixx stops at the edge of the grey dust fan in front of the burned arch. His toes are right at the line where the kobold prints stop. The boot prints go on past him, softened by ten days of draught, in under the blackened hinges.

You asked him on the way why the Broom won't go in, and he answers it now, looking into the dark of the arch and not at any of you.

"No ghosts," he says first, as if he's been asked that before. "Old ones say no ghosts. Is only old." He points his snout at the dark. "Tall shelves. Tall as Bram, taller. He thinks, and adds the part he plainly finds strangest.

"The four went in. String sang. Middle of the sleep. Broom woke and came out, and the four were in the paper room already, with lamps. Broom waited here, at the dust. Long. Lamps went far in. He steps back from the dust fan, one step and then another, until he's beside Hrask at the hides. He looks at the boot prints going in and not out, then at the three of you.

"Ixx waits here. Ixx sweeps the dust after, if the tall ones come out."

Under the arch the dark smells of old burned paper and nothing else. The shield-light reaches a stride in and finds the edge of a shelf: tall, black, leaning a little to the left.

Where you are: the dome, at the dust fan before the burned arch · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram stands at the edge of the dust and stares into the burned room, past his own shield-light. He looks over his shoulder at Ixx, then at you.

"If they didn't come out here, then there's a way from that room into the hot rooms," he says. "That's how they got behind us, or would have. That's where we look." He shifts his grip on the shield and hooks a thumb at the leaning shelf. "And that means we don't go leaning through there like men hunting deer. We find the way through with our eyes first, and we don't let the shelves block the way back."

He glances at Sefa. "Light close. Pell, watch the floor for scrape-lines and for anything shiny—bronze, iron, broken shelf. I'll lead and watch the beams. If I stop, we all stop."

Sefa stands at the edge of the dust fan a moment, looking at the boot prints going in and not coming out.

"Then they didn't walk across the hot rooms at all," she says, low, to Bram and you. "They went *in here*, far in, and came out on the bright side — at that old door Ixx won't look at, where the little fire stood up and lit itself for us. That's how they reached the rim without the Broom seeing them cross. They cut the plate, the light bit, they ran *back* the way they'd come — toward the old door, not the stair — and the floor took them short of it." She looks at the dark under the hinges. "So the piece is either in this room, on the far side, or in the bright cracks between the smear and that door. The Broom swept the pale side ten times and found nothing because it was never on the pale side."

She turns to Ixx and Hrask. "Thank you. Stay by the small ones. If we're not out by the time the fire's burned down a cake, don't come in after us — send Skra up the stair as far as the bend and leave her there." She nods to you. "Light your lantern; mine has a quarter hour and I'd rather not put the Lantern's colour on every shelf in a dead wizard's library before I know what's written in here. Bram, shield up and watch what leans — Tisk's egg-brother died under one of these, and you're the tallest thing in the room. Pell, the prints. I'll read."

Bram takes a step into the old library, careful as he was on the stairs, and lets the lamp throw its yellow across the shelves and the dust. The dry smell of burned paper rises around you like old smoke woken by your passing.

"Talk low," he says. "Sound carries in a room this old. If there's a way through, I want to find it before it finds us."

Ixx looks down at the grey fan of dust and then at you. He lifts his broom off the floor and holds it upright against his chest, well away from the dust.

"Ixx leaves it," he says. To Sefa he gives a single click and then remembers to say it in words. "Stays by small ones. Skra to the bend." Hrask says nothing. He has heard the shape of it, and his eyes go to the stack of dung cakes by the fire as if he's already counting them.

You open the shutter of your hooded lantern and hold it low at the arch, and the dark under the hinges turns brown and grey. The first shelf is as tall as Bram and half again. Its uprights are oak, charred black on the side that faced the fire, and they're set into iron shoes on the floor that have rusted to scale. It leans left by about a hand's width at the top, and the lean is held by a crossbar wedged against its neighbour. That's an old repair or a lucky fall, and either way it has held a long time. The shelves are full of what used to be books. They're black blocks now, fused to each other along the spines, and the edges have gone soft and grey like the ash at the end of a cigar. The draught from the dome stirs them, and a little drifts down. The boot prints run straight between the first two shelves, down the middle of the aisle. The four men walked where the floor was clear and touched nothing, and you can read that in the dust too: the ash on the shelf-edges along the aisle hasn't been disturbed.

Bram goes in first. His shield-light runs up the shelves and loses itself in the dark of the ceiling. You are at his shoulder with the lantern, and Sefa comes last, setting her feet in your prints.

The library is bigger than the dome. The aisle runs straight back from the arch between rows of shelves, maybe ninety feet, with cross-aisles every twenty. Near the end of the second row the light on Bram's shield thins, wavers and goes out, a few minutes short of a quarter hour, as Sefa said it would. For a moment there's only your lantern, and the shelves seem to step closer.

Thirty feet in, a shelf has come down. It fell long ago, across the aisle and against the shelf opposite, and it lies there like a roof beam, so the aisle runs under it in a low triangle of dark. Under it the floor has been dug. Old claw-scrapes run through the ash, and books are pulled out and heaped to one side, gone so soft they've slumped into a single grey drift. The boot prints go straight under the beam, bent low; the heels dig deeper there. Bram watches the beam as he ducks under it. Where it rests on the other shelf the charred upright has split along its grain, and a line of pale wood shows in the split. It isn't moving. Fine ash sifts down onto his shield as the mail on his back passes under, and settles. Nobody breathes on it.

Sefa reads as you go, her eyes on the shelf-ends. Most of what was written here is gone, burned into the black blocks or flaked off the shelf-ends with the char. Still, there are scraps. A shelf-end on the third row has a strip of bronze tacked to it, its raised letters still standing. Further back there's another. Under that, burned into the wood of the shelf, someone long ago scratched a tally of days, the way a bored apprentice does. Your lantern finds one book that the fire missed. It's lying flat on a lower shelf, as if somebody pulled it out and laid it down, lettering still on what's left of its spine. It's closed. Nobody touches it.

Among the stacks, with the arch a dim grey square behind you and no red anywhere near, Sefa stops and says it quietly, word for word:

"When it flared, the voice said: *That light is mine. Take it back.*" A breath. "Not *open the door*. Not *free me*. *Take it back*. That's what I'm here for, whether I like the timing or not — and nothing in those words says the fire comes with it." Her hand rests on the Book at her belt. "One more thing. Mage Hand reaches thirty feet. If the piece is lying in a bright crack, nobody's boot goes near it — I'll lift it out from the pale side with a hand that can't burn. Now let's find where these four came out."

The library takes it in. The air is dead here, and it doesn't carry.

At the far end the aisle comes up against a wall of dressed stone, and the boot prints go to a door in it. It's stone too, a slab on bronze pins, and it stands open about a forearm's width. Nobody has burned it, and there's no char on it at all. Above it a short line is cut into the lintel, under a small version of Ulcaster's stepped tower. The cutting is crisp, protected all these centuries by the shelves that stood in front of it. Sefa reads it twice.

At the door Bram turns and looks back down the aisle past your lantern.

You set the lantern to the gap and look before anyone goes through. Then you read the floor, which is your work and Bram's, and the floor is plain.

The room is small, perhaps twenty feet square, with a low vault and reading desks of stone built into the walls. The fire never got in here. There are shelves, with real books on them, warped and foxed and leather gone hard, but books. Someone has camped on the floor. There are two bedrolls, unrolled and left, a tin lamp on its side with its oil long burned off, and a heel of black bread gone stone-hard. A leather pack lies against the leg of the nearest desk, its flap open, and the corner of something folded in oilskin shows out of it. Beside it, flat on the stone, is a pair of heavy leather gloves. One is scorched brown across the palm.

On the far side of the room a second opening, square-topped and narrow like the old door across the hall, gives onto steps going down. Warm air comes up them, and the struck-flint smell with it. The prints tell the story the room won't. Four sets of boots come in from the library, walk around the camp and go down those steps together. One set comes back up. It's long-strided and scuffed, with the toes digging in, a man taking steps two at a time. It crosses straight to the desk where the pack lies and stops there. The heel marks turn on the spot. Then the same boots go back down the steps the way they came, running again.

Your lantern is turned toward the steps. Behind it, by the desk leg, between the pack and the scorched glove, there's a light where there shouldn't be one.

It's very faint, no more than a coal at the bottom of a grate. It's yellow, lamp-yellow, and it isn't your lantern's.

Where you are: the Apprentices' Room, beyond the burned library · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram stays still at the threshold, his eyes on the yellow light near the pack. "Sefa," he says quietly. "That's not firelight. That's something else, and it's sat right where one running man stopped, at the desk. Pell—hold where you are. Nobody touches that pack or the glove until we know what that light's coming from."

His shield stays up. "The four came in from the library, camped here, went down that stair together. He points with his chin at the single line of boot-prints on the floor, then at the oilskin sticking out of the pack. "That's where their own gear lies. Sefa stops in the doorway with one hand on the cold stone of the jamb. "Pell. Lower the lantern a moment. By the desk leg — between the pack and the glove." Her voice is barely above the dead air. "That's not your light, and it isn't mine. It's the colour of the thing on his door."

She reads the floor aloud: "Four went down those steps. One came back up — fast, two at a time — straight to this desk, stopped, turned on the spot, and went back *down*. Running. Not up to the stair, not out through the library. Down, toward the others." She looks at the scorched glove. "He had the piece in his hand and it was burning him through the leather.
